Your step-by-step course for building a property rental business for passive income, even without owning property.

Continue where you left off→

Welcome

We’re so happy you’re here. This course is everything we’ve learned in almost 10 years of hosting, turned into clear steps you can follow at your own pace.

Imagine having beautiful homes around the world. Places you can stay, rent out, and return to anytime. If you’ve ever dreamed of creating a business that gives you freedom, flexibility and income without being tied to a desk or needing to own real estate, this course is for YOU.

We created this course to help you launch, run and scale a profitable hosting business that works for you, not the other way around. Inside, you’ll find a step-by-step roadmap built from real experience. It teaches you how we did it and how you can too.

IMPORTANT

Section 1

Overview of the course

In Part 1, we lay the foundation. You’ll learn about the different business models (including how to start without buying property), how to get legally set up, build the right mindset and find your first profitable property even if pitching landlords makes you nervous.

In Part 2, we focus on launching your listing and welcoming your first guests. You’ll learn how to set up and furnish your listing, write a profile that sells, and manage your space efficiently with streamlined systems.

In Part 3, we scale it up to 6 figures. Learn how to automate tasks, build your dream team and expand without burning out. This is where your listing becomes a true business that generates passive income.

We’ve included everything you need: ready-to-use templates, calculators, scripts, real case studies and tools that remove the guesswork and save you hours.

Let’s build something profitable, sustainable, and designed for the lifestyle you actually want.

Section 2

How to use this course

This course is designed to walk you step by step through launching and growing your hosting business. You’ll find clear instructions, practical tasks, and real-world strategies that have been tested and refined over years of experience.

At certain points, you’ll be given specific action tasks to complete. You can find all of them organized inside your launch roadmap, here in the course. Use it to stay on track, mark your progress, and avoid feeling overwhelmed.

You’ll also see ready-to-use AI prompts throughout the course. They help you write faster and get better results with less effort.

Use this course as your playbook. Take it one step at a time, stay consistent, and don’t let small setbacks slow you down.

Take action along the way
  • Every lesson ends with your tasks. Tick them off and the progress bar at the top moves.
  • Every prompt and template has a Copy button, so you can simply copy and paste it into your favorite AI tool (like ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude). Type your details once (like your city) and the course adds them to every prompt for you.
Choose your currency
This changes the currency everywhere in the course, like the setup checklist, the profit calculator and the AI prompts. You can change it anytime.
Section 3

Do you have what it takes?

Running a hosting business can be fun, rewarding and highly profitable, but it also takes the right mindset.

The truth is, things will occasionally get damaged. Sometimes you have to deal with bad guests, but it’s part of the game. That’s why you have a team that helps you, and why Airbnb offers host protection.

99% of the guests are amazing, respectful, kind, and grateful, but there is always that 1% who cause problems, complain unfairly, or try to get a discount by pointing out minor flaws. But honestly, it’s all worth it.

“99% of the guests you’ll receive are awesome, but oh, that 1%…”

Also remember, people are out of their usual routine. They might be jet-lagged, hungry, tired, or stressed and sometimes they will react in a totally unreasonable way. Your job (or your manager’s) is not to take things personally, and to stay calm and professional.

You’ll learn so much along the way: not just about hosting, but about people. It’s fascinating to see how different guests are, how cultures interact, and how you grow by learning to stay calm in unexpected situations.

This journey will challenge you, shape you, and help you grow both as a business owner and as a person.

Besides the profit, the experience alone is worth it. Building a business is one of the best forms of self-development you can ever give yourself.

In the beginning, things like a bad review or a difficult guest might affect you a lot. But with every situation you handle, you become stronger and more resilient, and after a while you’ll deal with them much more easily.

Dealing with a difficult guest? We have a dedicated lesson: Difficult guests.

Introduction · Farah & Daniel

Our story

From being broke and sleeping on the couch to a 6-figure business that runs by itself and multiple homes around the world.

about 5 minLesson00
01 We both left our hometown with our entire life in a suitcase

In our early twenties, we both left our home countries behind (Belgium and Brazil) and moved to Barcelona with nothing but a suitcase, a little savings, and a whole lot of uncertainty. No safety net. No family nearby. Just the belief that there had to be more to life than doing things the “normal” way.

02 In 2017, Farah rented a room from Daniel

Daniel was living in a tiny room while he was renting out the bigger rooms of his shared rental apartment. It was actually a walk-in closet with no exterior windows, turned into a bedroom. Farah rented one of those bigger rooms, and that’s how we met: as housemates in a shared apartment, both trying to make ends meet in one of Europe’s most expensive cities.

03 Farah got her own rental apartment (and ended up broke)

After a few months, Farah moved into her own place. After paying a huge deposit and buying the basics, she had only €67.50 left in her bank account. She even found some of her furniture on the street and made a bed from pallets. Rent was high, savings were gone, and things were getting tight. Going back to cold Belgium because the money ran out? She wasn’t going to let that happen. So she got creative.

Farah sublet her bedroom and sometimes slept on the couch, behind a giant beach blanket she hung from a hook above the fridge to the curtain railing by the window. It wasn’t glamorous, but it worked.

04 The “wait a second…” moment: let’s go all in

At first, it was just a way to help pay the rent. But soon we realized… WAIT. We can actually make serious money doing this?!

So we went ALL IN.

We couldn’t afford a team yet, so we both did everything ourselves: cleaning, check-ins, guest messages and maintenance, even watching YouTube tutorials on how to fix a toilet.

05 We built systems and started working smarter, not harder

We set up self-check-in and automated messages, and hired our first cleaner. Every euro we made, we reinvested, and we made sacrifices. We also upgraded the furniture and made every room more beautiful for a better guest experience. Little by little, the business started running without needing us 24/7.

And THAT changed everything.

06 We officially opened a company and even got our dream rooftop apartment

One apartment turned into two, then five.

When the rules became stricter in Barcelona, we adapted. No tourist stays: we offer mid-term stays of 31+ nights, which is 100% legal without needing a license. Literally anyone is allowed to rent out monthly stays in Barcelona (even on Airbnb), but not many people know this.

We don’t own any property. We work with local owners. We make a profit by renting big apartments with many bedrooms that are hard for them to rent out, and subletting the rooms individually with the owner’s permission.

We know how hard it can be to move alone to a new city, because we’ve been there ourselves. In Barcelona, scams are a real issue, and we’ve been through them: fake listings, lost deposits, endless paperwork, and dirty shared apartments with zero organization.

That’s why our mission is to offer a ready-to-move-in home to students, digital nomads and anyone living abroad, so they can simply arrive and start enjoying the city.

07 Then came the big one: our dream villa in Bali

We put all our savings into a very basic villa in Bali. Scary AF. We renovated it, made it beautiful and turned it into a mini luxury boutique hotel with three bedrooms.

We also officially opened a company in Bali and built a team here too. And the wildest part? We now have rental properties in different parts of the world, and we still don’t own a single one of them.

08 We didn’t just build an income stream. We built freedom.

Fast forward almost 10 years: we run a profitable business with multiple properties around the world and a consistent passive income. And we started literally from zero.

We believe that if you put love into your business, it comes right back to you. So we overpay our staff, work with the local communities, and set up our properties to give our guests an amazing 5-star experience. It’s a win-win.

09 Now we teach you how

When we started, we had no idea what we were doing. We learned everything the hard way, by trial and error and a lot of late nights.

This course is everything we wish someone had told us back then. It’s step by step and built from real-life experience, not just theory. Our course is designed to be your shortcut to business success.

Whether you want some extra income, homes in different places around the world, or a business that gives you more freedom, we’ll show you how, so you can build your own property rental business without making the same mistakes we did.

Will it always be easy? No. Is it possible? 100%.

Part 1 · Lesson 1

Choose your business model

Even without owning property.

3 sections · about 15 minLesson01
Section 1

Rental arbitrage vs co-hosting vs ownership

If you’ve ever wanted to start your own business but thought you’d need a fortune to begin, this might be exactly what you’ve been looking for. Most people assume a hosting business means buying property, taking out a mortgage or saving for years. It doesn’t.

In reality, some of the most profitable hosts don’t own a single property, and neither do we.

There are different ways to make money as a host.

There are three main business models: rental arbitrage, co-hosting and ownership. With rental arbitrage and co-hosting, you can launch your hosting business without buying property. You don’t need a mortgage or a big down payment. What you do need is strategy and the right systems.

How much you need to start depends on the model. With co-hosting, you can start with almost no money, because you manage someone else’s property.

With rental arbitrage, you do need some budget. Before your first guest arrives, you pay the deposit, the first month’s rent and the furniture to make the place guest-ready.

To give you an idea: for our apartments in Barcelona, we needed roughly €10,000 to get started. Your number depends on the property and the location. It’s still a fraction of what buying would cost, and once you’re booked, you earn it back fast.

Already own a property? Even better. You’re sitting on an asset that can earn you money. By renting it out on a platform like Airbnb or Booking.com, you can earn much more from it, whether it’s a second home, an investment property or even just a spare room.

With the right setup, it can become a steady source of passive income.

Here is an overview of the most common business models. Tap the one that fits you.

Your tasks
Section 2

Mid-term vs short-term rentals

Choose the type of stay that fits your goals, your location and your lifestyle.

Mid-term rentals

Guests stay 1 to 6 months (sometimes longer): mostly students, digital nomads, expats, people relocating for work, and travelers on a long vacation.

Short-term rentals

Bookings range from 1 night up to a few weeks: mostly tourists on holiday, plus weekend trips and business travelers.

Here is how the two compare.

Mid-termShort-term
Stay length1 to 6 months (sometimes longer)1 night up to a few weeks
Typical guestsStudents, digital nomads, expats, people relocating, long vacationsMostly tourists, plus weekend trips and business travelers
IncomeLower nightly rate, but steady and predictableHigher nightly rates, with more ups and downs
WorkloadLow: few turnovers and lower cleaning costsHigher: frequent cleaning and guest messages
Your calendarLess flexible: one guest can take the whole monthMore flexible, more control, and more visibility in search results
Wear and tearGuests live there like at home and may ask for more maintenanceGuests are out exploring most of the day, but expect the occasional difficult guest
Local rulesOften the option that works where short stays are restrictedOften needs a license or permit
Best forSteady, passive income with minimal workMaximum profit, with strong systems in place

Choose your type of stay

Tap the one that fits you best.

Not sure yet? You can also combine both: short-term in high season and mid-term in low season, as long as the local rules allow it.

Your tasks
Section 3

Shared vs private properties

The second choice is what guests actually book: the entire place, one room, or both.

Private properties

Guests have exclusive use of an entire unit or suite, with a private entrance, bedroom and bathroom.

Shared spaces

Guests rent a room in a larger unit and share the common areas (kitchen, pool, living room).

Good to know: “coliving”. Most people who run shared spaces call it coliving. It’s the same setup: private rooms, shared common areas. In cities with stricter rules and more tension around short-term rentals, presenting your place as a coliving space can make conversations easier.

List both ways

You list the same property in two ways at once: as an entire place, and room by room. This is the format we usually run ourselves.

One property has several listings: one for the whole property and one for each bedroom. A family or a group of friends can book the entire place. A solo traveler or a couple can book just one room and share the kitchen, living room or pool with other guests. Whichever booking comes in first takes the dates.*

*The calendars must be linked. If one room is booked, the whole property is blocked for those dates, and the other way around. Otherwise you risk a double booking.

Here is how the three compare.

PrivateSharedBoth ways
Guests bookThe entire placeOne room, sharing the common areasEither the whole place or one room
PriceHighest per nightLower per booking, but more per square meterFlexible: you sell it both ways and see what earns more
OccupancyOne booking at a timeHigh demand, because it’s more affordable for travelersHighest: rooms fill the gaps a whole-place booking leaves
GuestsPreferred by most travelers: better reviews, fewer complaintsGreat for solo and social guests, but a higher chance of noise or conflictsWorks for groups and families as well as solo travelers
CostsHigher: you furnish and maintain the entire spaceLower per guestThe same furniture, team and setup serve both
EffortEasiest: expectations are simpleMore house rules, labels and clear communicationThe most setup: more listings to manage, and minimum stays and pricing need more thought
Best forA broad market of travelersBackpacker and digital nomad hotspotsProperties with several bedrooms

Choose your setup

Tap the one that fits you best.

There’s no one-size-fits-all. The key is to choose deliberately, based on your location, your personality, your target market and the systems you’re willing to build.

Part 1 · Lesson 2

Legal & local rules

The boring stuff (that keeps your business safe).

2 sections · about 15 minLesson02
Section 1

Understanding local rules

Rules around property rentals vary widely depending on where you are, but this also offers opportunities. In general, cities with more tourism tend to have stricter regulations due to housing shortages, tourism limits, and local government control.

Cities like Barcelona, Paris, New York City, and Amsterdam often require licenses, limit the number of rental nights, or restrict short-term rentals to certain zones.

That doesn't mean strictly regulated places are a no-go. We currently run multiple successful apartments in Barcelona, one of the most difficult cities for Airbnb. They don’t have a tourist license, but they’re all still legal.

In Barcelona, anyone is allowed to create a listing on a platform like Airbnb without a license, as long as you host stays of 31 nights or more. Not many people know this, and that’s exactly the opportunity.

While monthly stays tend to generate less income per night than short-term bookings, they’re still highly profitable. Plus, they come with fewer guest turnovers, less day-to-day management, and more stability. You might not even need a manager or a full-time team.

On the other hand, some areas are much more flexible and easier to start in. Places like Bali, parts of Mexico, Portugal, and Southern Spain are known for being more open to short-term rentals, especially in tourist-friendly zones or when offering longer stays. This is why choosing the right location is key.

Before you list any property, it's crucial to understand the local laws and regulations in your area. Every city has its own rules when it comes to short-term rentals. Some require specific licenses or permits, others have restrictions on the number of nights you can rent, and some zones may not allow short-term rentals at all.

Rule typeWhat it meansExample
Minimum stay requirementsSome cities only allow short-term rentals if stays are longer than a specific number of days.Barcelona: Only allowed if the stay is 31+ days unless you have a tourist license
Tourist license or permitMany cities require a special license to operate legally.Paris: Requires registration number and permit for short-term rentals
Zoning restrictionsNot all areas within a city allow short-term rentals.New York City: Some buildings and zones prohibit short-term listings entirely
Primary residence requirementIn some cities, you can only rent out your primary residence and not an investment property.San Francisco: Must be your primary residence and registered with the city
Limit on rental nightsSome places limit how many nights per year you can rent out a property.London: Max 90 nights per year without a permit
Co-op and HOA rulesApartment buildings and homeowner associations may have their own restrictions.Varies: Always check building policies separately from city laws
AI prompt: discover the local rental rules in your area
Can you help me find the current rules for renting out a property in ? I want to understand the rules for short-term rentals (under 1 month), mid-term rentals (1 to 6 months) and long-term rentals, and for subletting a property I rent (rental arbitrage). For each type of rental, I want to know: - If it is legal, and under which conditions - Whether I need a license, permit or registration - Any minimum or maximum stay rules, or limits on the number of nights per year - Tax obligations (income tax, tourist or occupancy tax) - Zoning restrictions, primary residence rules or building/HOA rules - What a landlord needs to agree to if I want to sublet - Whether I can do this as a private individual, or need to register as self-employed or a company Please include any helpful links or resources to official government sites if available. At the end, add a short summary I can copy into my notes, in this format: - Short-term rentals (under 1 month): allowed / not allowed / with conditions - Mid-term rentals (1–6 months): allowed / not allowed / with conditions - Long-term rentals: allowed / not allowed / with conditions - Subletting (rental arbitrage): allowed / not allowed / with conditions - License or permit needed: yes / no (and which one) - Minimum stay: ... - Taxes: ... - Other important rules: ...

Your tasks
Section 2

Legal setup: private, self-employed or company?

Let’s be real, no one gets excited about legal paperwork. Luckily, you don’t need a complicated legal setup to get started. But it’s important to know your options and to declare your income from day one.

You have three main options: rent out as a private individual, start as self-employed, or register a company. Which one fits depends on your country, what you offer your guests and how big you want to grow.

Option 1: rent out as a private individual

Many people don’t know this: in many countries you can rent out a place as a private person, without registering as self-employed or opening a company. You simply declare the rental income on your personal tax return once a year, and you can usually deduct costs like rent, utilities, furniture and cleaning.

This usually works when:

  • You only rent out the space. Cleaning between guests, keys and basic maintenance are normal for any landlord.
  • You don’t offer hotel-like services during the stay, such as a reception, daily cleaning, meals, laundry or airport transfers.
  • You keep it small: one or a few listings, and no staff on your payroll.

Once you start offering hotel-like services or grow into a real operation with staff, tax authorities usually see it as a business. Then you need to register as self-employed or open a company, and in some countries you also charge VAT.

Example: how it works
SpainIf you rent out an apartment you own without hotel-like services, you declare it as rental income in your yearly income tax return (IRPF). No need to become autónomo. If you sublet a place you rent (rental arbitrage), the income is also taxed in your yearly return, unless it’s run as a business. Offer hotel-like services and it becomes a business: you register as autónomo and usually charge 10% VAT.
BelgiumIf you rent out one or a few places without extra services, you can do it as a private individual. You declare it on your yearly tax return: for the property, tax is based on its cadastral income (kadastraal inkomen), and if it’s furnished, 40% of the rent counts as income from the furniture. Offer services like breakfast or cleaning during the stay, and do it regularly? Then it becomes a professional activity: you register as self-employed (this can be a side activity, zelfstandige in bijberoep) and usually charge 6% VAT.
United StatesMost hosts report their rental income as rental income on Schedule E, without self-employment tax. If you provide substantial services, like daily cleaning, meals or concierge, it counts as a business (Schedule C).

Always declare your income. Since 2023, platforms like Airbnb and Booking.com share hosts’ income with the tax authorities for every listing in the EU. Renting out as a private individual doesn’t mean tax-free: it just means less admin.

Option 2 and 3: self-employed or a company

When you’re growing, offering hotel-like services or hiring a team, it’s time for an official setup.

CategorySelf-employedRegister an official company
Best forGetting started quickly with low risk and minimal costsScaling your business, hiring people, and protecting yourself legally
Pros• Easy and cheap to register
• Less paperwork and admin
• Great for testing the waters		• Separates personal & business assets
• More credibility with landlords and banks
• Possible tax advantages
• Easier to partner or raise capital
Cons• No legal separation
• You’re personally liable
• Might seem less professional		• More complex setup
• Ongoing admin and costs
• Likely need an accountant
Ideal forIf you’re just starting or managing 1–2 listings with servicesIf you’re growing fast, managing multiple properties, or hiring a team

Choose your setup

Tap the one that fits you best.

How to double-check before you decide

The rules are different in every country, so don’t rely on one source. Follow these steps to be sure:

  1. Start with AI. Use the AI prompt in Section 1 to get a quick overview. It’s a great starting point, but AI can be wrong or out of date.
  2. Check your tax office’s website. Search for “renting out property” or “rental income” on the official site, for example the Agencia Tributaria in Spain, the FOD Financiën / SPF Finances in Belgium or the IRS in the US. Many tax offices also have a free helpline or chat.
  3. Check your city or region for licenses and registration. That’s a separate question from taxes.
  4. Talk to a local accountant or tax advisor (in Spain: a gestor or asesor fiscal). Tell them exactly what you plan to do: own or rented property, how long guests stay, and whether you offer extra services.
  5. Get the answer in writing. Ask for it by email and keep it with your documents.

Part 1 · Lesson 3

Think like a business owner, not just a host

Mindset, extra income and the tools you need.

4 sections · about 5 minLesson03
Section 1

Overcoming fear of getting started

Getting started is often the hardest part. It’s completely normal to feel uncertain, nervous, or even overwhelmed when stepping into something new. You might be thinking, “What if something goes wrong?” or “Am I really ready for this?” These doubts are common, but they’re also what keep most people stuck on the sidelines.

The truth is, no one feels fully ready in the beginning. Every successful host once stood exactly where you are now: unsure, questioning themselves, and wondering if they could actually do it. What made the difference is that they took action anyway.

Many people also feel resistance to pitching landlords, afraid they’ll say no. But many owners want exactly what you offer: rent paid on time and a well-kept property. You only need one yes, and Lesson 6 gives you the scripts.

If you want to succeed, you need to shift your mindset from being just a host to thinking like a business owner. Becoming a 6-figure host isn’t just about giving someone a nice place to sleep. If you want to make real money, it’s about creating systems, solving problems, managing relationships, and building something that can grow. A business owner makes decisions based on vision and long-term goals, not just today’s to-do list.

You don’t need to have it all figured out. You just need to start. Follow the steps in this course, one task at a time. You’ll learn by doing, gain confidence as you go, and build momentum with every small win.

Yes, you’ll face challenges. And yes, mistakes will happen. But every problem has a solution, and every obstacle is an opportunity to get better. Confidence doesn’t come from waiting until you’re ready. It comes from showing up anyway.

So take a deep breath, trust yourself, and begin. You’re not just launching a listing. You’re building a business that can change your life.

Section 2

Think big: our most profitable apartment

Thinking like a business owner also means looking at a property for what it could be, not for what it is today. Here are two of our apartments in Barcelona that taught us this the most.

Case study · BarcelonaHow an ugly apartment became our most profitable one

This is our most profitable apartment. When we took it, it was very ugly. The first thing we did was paint everything white. Then we added two bedrooms, super easily, by putting in one simple plasterboard (drywall) wall.

See how huge the living room was? On the right side, the part we circled, is where we added two bedrooms.

On the left, the living room after we painted it. On the right, the same side we circled in the before picture: the new white wall with two doors is what we added.

Two extra rooms from one simple wall

Those two extra rooms make us around €1,600 extra a month, and as you can see, they don’t even have an exterior window. They have a small inner window to the living room.

These are the two bedrooms we added behind the new wall. The window with the arrow is an inner window to the living room, not an exterior window.

It was Daniel’s idea. The first time he told Farah, she said: “No way, that’s crazy.” Today, these are some of our most popular rooms, because a lot of people in Barcelona have a smaller budget and are looking for exactly a room like this.

Six rooms need more than one bathroom

With six bedrooms, one bathroom would never have been enough. So we turned the old laundry area into an extra shower room. Now there are never issues, even with many people living in the apartment.

Pretty sells

Just by making it aesthetic and pretty, you can ask 20% to 30% more, without doing a crazy renovation. White walls, warm lights, simple wooden furniture and nice bedding do most of the work.

Our smallest room is our most popular one

We even have one bedroom that is super small. It has no window, not even an inner window. And it’s our most popular bedroom, just because the price is lower, and a lot of people are looking in that budget.

Think big. Maybe you would not want to stay there, but other people do.

For a lot of people, it’s a dream to live in a beautiful, big apartment like this, with balconies, in the centre of Barcelona, even if their own bedroom is small and has no window. Don’t judge a room by your own standards. Look at what your guests are looking for, and at the budget they have.

Before you build a wall or add a bedroom, agree it with the owner in writing and check your local rules on what counts as a bedroom. How we pitched this type of apartment to the landlord is in Lesson 6.

Case study · BarcelonaOne extra bedroom in the living room: +€900 a month

This is another of our apartments in Barcelona. When it was time to extend the contract, we didn’t just want to renew it. We also wanted to add an extra bedroom in the living room, so we could rent out one more room and make more profit.

The big living room before. Beautiful, but most of it was empty space.

After: the kitchen and dining area are still there, and next to them the new bedroom, with its own balcony.

Why we did it

We noticed that most people who rent an individual bedroom spend very little time in the shared areas. They mostly stay in their own room. So even though a very big living room looks great, it doesn’t earn anything. One more bedroom means one more guest, and one more rent every month.

It was Daniel’s idea, and Farah thought he was crazy. Today, this room earns us around €900 extra a month.

Empty space doesn’t pay. A bedroom does.

As with any change to the layout, agree it with the owner in writing first. Here we did it as part of extending the contract.

Section 3

Creative ways to make extra money (optional)

Being a host isn’t just about charging for a night’s stay. You can boost your income by offering extra services and experiences, many of which run on their own. Here are some creative ideas:

  • Local partners and referral commissions: Work with local businesses and earn a commission every time you send them a guest. Think of tour operators, surf lessons, motorbike rentals, restaurants, and websites with referral (affiliate) programs for event tickets and activities. Your guests get trusted recommendations and you get paid for them. We earned commission, for example, selling tickets for Barcelona parties to our guests. It was around €10 per ticket, and in summer about 60% of our guests bought them, because it was an activity made for them.
  • Airport transfers: Guests often prefer a smooth arrival, especially in unfamiliar destinations. Partner with a reliable local driver to offer airport pick-up. Add a commission for yourself or bundle it as a premium add-on.
  • Floating breakfasts (especially in Bali): If your property has a pool, a beautiful floating breakfast is a popular experience. It creates shareable content for guests and earns you extra without much work. You can partner with a local café or set up your own simple breakfast tray.

The key is to think about what fits naturally with your property and your lifestyle. These add-ons can increase your income, improve guest satisfaction, and build a more memorable hosting brand with very little extra effort.

Section 4

Must-have business tools for hosts

Here’s an overview of the must-have apps, websites, and tools to run your hosting business like a pro. Don’t worry, we’ll explain each one later in this course, so you know exactly what to use and how to set it up.

Part 1 · Lesson 4

Do market research

Find out where guests want to stay, what they pay and when they come.

4 sections · about 15 minLesson04
Section 1

Location vs demand

what actually drives bookings

Most people think location is everything. It isn’t. A prime spot helps, but demand is what fills your calendar.

Fixed

Location

Where your property is. You can’t change it.

Dynamic

Demand

What people search for, when and why. This is what you can play with.

The plot twist: a great location with low demand will struggle. A less obvious location with high demand and the right setup? That’s a goldmine.

Demand comes from two places

1

Demand for the area

Guests come for the city, the beach, a university, a hospital or an event. You compete with every listing around you.

  • A beach town 20 minutes from a popular city can beat a central apartment on weekend getaways.
  • A quiet suburb near a hospital or university stays booked by nurses, researchers and digital nomads.
2

Demand for the property itself

The one most new hosts miss: many guests travel for the stay, not the city. They’ll happily drive an extra hour to get it.

  • A cabin in the woods with no phone signal
  • A villa in the rice fields with a private pool and total silence
  • A design house in a tiny village, booked for birthdays
  • A farm stay with a hot tub, a fireplace and animals
1 of 1When the property is the reason for the trip, you’re not one of 300 similar apartments. You’re the only place like yours, and a “bad” location becomes the selling point.

Ask these 5 questions about every property

1

Who is coming here, and why?

2

Would they come for the area, or for this property?

3

When is demand highest?

4

Which stays are most common: weekends, short trips or monthly moves?

5

If the location is average, what could make the stay special? A view, a pool, a hot tub, the design, total privacy?

Check the data: use AirROI and Airbnb’s filters to compare occupancy, nightly rates and competition. Then search for unusual stays nearby and see how booked their calendars are.
The goal

The right property for the right guest: in a place people already want to be, or special enough that people come for it.

Section 2

How to use AirROI

to analyze profit potential

Before committing to a property, you need to know one thing: Will it actually make money?

AirROI is the tool we recommend for this research. It shows you what a short-term rental can earn in a specific place, based on real booking data. Its calculator and market data are free to use.

Step-by-step:

  1. Go to AirROI.com and open the Calculator
  2. Type in the address (or the area) you're researching and the number of bedrooms
  3. AirROI compares it with around 50 comparable properties nearby and shows you:
    • What a short-term rental there could earn
    • Month-by-month income projections
    • The comparable listings it used
  4. Add your operating costs to go from income to net income
  5. Open the market map to explore the area and compare neighborhoods
  6. Take the nightly price and occupancy you found into your Profit Calculator

Even with great data, don’t rely on just one source. Cross-check with Airbnb itself, Booking.com, or local Facebook rental groups. If two sources give you very different numbers for the same property, be careful and use the lower one.

Understanding the numbers upfront is key to building a profitable hosting business. Use the data, not guesswork, to guide your choices.

Your tasks
Section 3

Market research with AI

Today you can also do this research with AI. An AI assistant that can search the web can pull together nightly prices, occupancy and the type of traveler who visits your area in just a few minutes.

Use it as a second source next to AirROI, not instead of it. Fill in the brackets, copy the prompt and paste it into your AI assistant.

AI prompt: market research for your area
Act as a short-term rental market analyst and search the web for current data. I'm looking at a in , , to rent out as . Give me, in one short table each: 1. Nightly prices for similar listings (low, typical, high) in high and low season 2. Occupancy by month, and which months are high and low season 3. Who travels here, why, and what they expect from a place Then tell me in three lines whether this looks like a good opportunity and what would make this property stand out. Name the source for every number, and say clearly when you are estimating. If you need more details from me, ask up to three questions before you answer.
Copy and open in:ChatGPTGeminiClaude

AI can get numbers wrong or use old data. Check the nightly prices against real listings on Airbnb, and compare the occupancy with AirROI before you put anything into your Profit Calculator.

Your tasks
Section 4

Research directly on Airbnb

The best free research tool is Airbnb itself. Search your area the way a guest would. In 20 minutes you know your competition, the real prices and what guests care about.

Step-by-step:

1

Search like a guest

Open Airbnb and zoom the map in until it only shows your neighborhood.

2

Match your property

Entire place or room, number of bedrooms, number of guests.

3

Compare the dates

Weekday vs weekend, 1 vs 3 months ahead, high vs low season. Write down the low, typical and high price.

4

Check 5 to 10 calendars

Lots of blocked dates usually mean good demand. Hosts can block dates too, so look at several listings.

5

Count the recent reviews

Many recent reviews = a listing that gets booked regularly.

6

Study the Guest favorites

Cover photo, title, amenities and price. That’s the bar you have to match or beat.

7

Read the reviews, good and bad

Guests tell you exactly what they loved and what was missing. Free ideas for your own listing.

What to look for

A gap in the market

Lots of similar apartments, but nothing for groups, with a workspace or a pool? That gap can be your listing.

Too much competition

Hundreds of similar listings with open calendars and low prices is a warning sign.

The price guests really pay

Totals can include cleaning and service fees. Compare totals, not just the nightly price.

Do this search again every few months, also after you launch. Prices, competition and what guests expect change all the time.

Part 1 · Lesson 5

Find the right property

Where to find units, red flags and the numbers.

4 sections · about 15 minLesson05
Section 1

How to find the right property

Good news: you don’t need special “Airbnb-friendly” listings. For rental arbitrage, normal rental listings on normal property websites are your hunting ground. You rent the place the normal way, but you come with a better offer.

Heads-up: for many owners this will be the first time they hear about this. That’s normal. Your job is to explain it clearly and make them feel safe. Lesson 6 shows you how.
1

Start with the legal rules

Know what’s allowed in your area (Lesson 2): short or mid-term stays, and whether you need a license. In Barcelona, for example, mid-term stays of 31+ nights work without one.

Always: the owner’s written permission to sublet, in the contract.

2

Look on the right platforms

  • Normal property rental websites, like Idealista, Fotocasa or your local equivalent
  • Facebook Marketplace & local groups (look for flexible landlords)
  • Furnished and mid-term rental platforms like Spotahome or Flatio
  • Real estate agencies (ask for owners who want a reliable long-term tenant)
  • Airbnb itself (reach out to owners who don’t live there; some are open to co-hosting deals)
  • Word of mouth or local connections (especially helpful in places like Bali or Portugal)
Your tasks
Section 2

Red flags to avoid when choosing a property

Not all properties are good for renting out to guests, whether you host short-term or mid-term stays, even if they look beautiful, cheap, or perfectly located. Some places come with hidden issues that can cost you time, money, and a ton of stress. The key is learning to spot these red flags before you commit.

Here’s what to watch out for:

1

Strict building rules or HOAs

If you’re looking at an apartment in a building with a homeowner’s association (HOA), make sure to ask about their rules for short-term rentals and subletting. Some buildings ban or heavily restrict short stays, while mid-term stays of a month or more are often fine. With short stays, a concierge or nosy neighbors will notice guest traffic quickly.

Red flag: Contracts that mention “no subletting,” “no commercial use,” or restrictions on guest frequency.
2

Uncooperative landlords or property managers

If a landlord seems uncomfortable with your plan or won’t give you permission in writing, don’t move forward. Vague verbal approvals won’t protect you if things go wrong. You want a clear agreement up front.

Red flag: Landlords who avoid the topic, say “let’s just see how it goes,” or refuse to put anything in writing.
3

Problematic neighbors or thin walls

Angry neighbors are one of the fastest ways to lose a listing. If you’re sharing walls with people who hate noise, guests, or strangers in the building, you’re asking for complaints and potential legal issues.

Red flag: Past conflicts in the building, complaints from other tenants, or extra-thin walls.
4

Bad layout or limited privacy

Guests value privacy, functionality, and comfort. Avoid properties with awkward layouts, no doors between sleeping areas, or bathrooms that feel exposed. This can lead to bad reviews and poor occupancy rates. Mid-term guests, like digital nomads, also need a good place to work and fast Wi-Fi.

Red flag: Studios trying to act like 2-bedrooms, shared bathrooms, or no soundproofing.
5

Hard-to-reach locations or no parking

Location isn’t just about being central. It’s about being convenient. If the property is hard to find, far from transport, or has zero parking, it could turn off potential guests. Mid-term guests, like students and remote workers, also want shops, cafés and public transport nearby.

Red flag: Remote areas with no public transport or city apartments with expensive or no parking options.
6

Too much personal stuff or damage

Properties that are still full of the owner's belongings, expensive artwork, or delicate furniture can be a headache. Hosting requires a space that’s guest-ready, durable, and easy to clean.

Red flag: Cluttered units, sentimental or fragile items, and spaces that aren’t fully “handed over.”
7

No track record

If the unit has never been rented before and the landlord is unsure, treat it as a test. Try a shorter lease, or ask for a trial period to minimize your risk.

Red flag: High rent, no data to support demand, or landlords who expect full-year commitment without flexibility.

Bottom line: It’s better to walk away from a risky deal than to regret it later. Trust your gut, do your research, and don’t compromise on legal clarity, location quality, or guest experience. A solid property sets the foundation for a stress-free, profitable hosting business.

Section 3

Calculate costs and profit potential

What it really costs to start (& how to keep it low)

Starting costs less than you think, especially if you don’t buy property.

Rental arbitrage

Your main costs: the first month’s rent, the deposit and furnishing the space.

Co-hosting

Close to zero. You work with someone else’s property.

Here are the typical startup costs for rental arbitrage:

  • First month’s rent
  • Security deposit (usually one month)
  • Furniture and essentials
  • Cleaning supplies
  • Photography (can be DIY with a good phone)
Do this

Keep costs low

  • Buy secondhand on Facebook Marketplace
  • Buy in bundles
  • Furnish slowly and upgrade as you earn
Focus on this

What guests really care about

  • A good bed
  • Fast Wi-Fi
  • A spotless space
  • Clear communication
How we built our business

Start small and reinvest your profits. Don’t overthink, don’t overspend, don’t chase perfect. Launch smart and upgrade as you grow.

Run your own numbers

Want to see what these costs mean for your profit? Use the Profit & ROI calculator. It lets you plug in expected costs, nightly rates, occupancy and other key numbers to estimate your monthly profit and return on investment. Use it to compare different properties, spot red flags and make smart, data-driven decisions.

Open the profit calculator
Your tasks
Section 4

Bonus: decision-making matrix for new properties

Before you commit to any property, you need to make sure it’s actually a smart investment. Instead of going off 'vibes' or falling in love with a nice kitchen, this tool helps you evaluate potential listings based on the things that really matter.

Score each category, add it up, and you’ll have a clear picture of whether it’s worth your time and money.

Decision-making matrix
Demand in the areaIs there high demand from guests (short- or mid-term), based on AirROI or local research?
Legal permissionAre short- or mid-term rentals legally allowed in this area?
Profit potentialWhat’s the estimated monthly profit after expenses? Use your ROI calculator to help.
Condition of the propertyIs it move-in ready or will it require major renovation or investment?
Upfront costsHow affordable is the deposit, furniture, and setup compared to your available budget?
Ease of managementWill check-ins, cleaning and guest support be easy to handle in this location?
Guest appealIs it photogenic, well-located, and likely to impress guests? Does it have unique features?
Landlord relationship (if not buying property)Is the landlord open to short- or mid-term rentals or rental arbitrage? Are they easy to communicate with and reliable?
Potential to scaleCould you potentially manage more units in this building or area later on?
Neighbors & communityAre neighbors friendly or tolerant toward guests? Is the building open to short- or mid-term rentals?

Part 1 · Lesson 6

Pitch landlords

If you want to legally sublet (rental arbitrage).

4 sections · about 25 minLesson06
Section 1

Why landlords say yes

(& how to position your offer)

Most people assume landlords say no to subletting. Many say yes, when your offer is positioned the right way.

Why? Because you're solving a real problem for them.

Every landlord wants 3 things

Incomereliable and on time
Carea well-kept home
Peaceas little stress as possible

Traditional tenants put all three at risk: late payments, poor communication, damage, even legal disputes.

What you offer

With rental arbitrage, you offer a smart alternative:

  • Consistent, on-time payments
  • Professional cleaning after every guest
  • Ongoing maintenance and inspections
  • Hands-off, well-organized management
Remember who you’re talking to: someone who rents out a property probably owns at least two. They’re often business-minded, and more open than you think when they see you run a serious business, not a side hustle.
1

Show your systems

Walk them through your cleaning checklist, message templates and SOPs (all in this course). You’re not winging it.

2

Respect the neighbors

You screen guests, enforce the house rules and keep quiet hours. Happy neighbors mean long-term success.

3

Your interest = their interest

Bad reviews kill bookings, so you need their home in top condition. You’ll take better care of it than most tenants ever would.

4

It’s a win-win

Position it right, and you’re not asking for permission. You’re offering a better deal.

Smart landlords would actually love to work with professional renters, because you solve their biggest headaches.

Focus on their biggest fear: bad tenants

Now compare that to renting to you, a professional renter. The landlord can count on:

  • Guaranteed rent, no late payments
  • A property kept in top condition
  • Professional cleaning after every stay
  • Instant expert repairs in case of damage
  • Exterior security cameras
  • Guest screening protocols
  • Regular property inspections

Your biggest argument to convince a landlord

The better you look after the property, the more 5‑star reviews you get, the more profit. You need the home to stay in excellent condition for this to work.

That’s why your interests and the landlord’s are the same: a guest who finds a dirty or damaged home leaves a bad review, and bad reviews cost you money. So you take better care of their property than almost any tenant would. Reviews like this one are what you work for:

It’s a win-win: they get zero headaches, and you get a home you can legally sublet for profit. But it won’t work if you just message them: “Hi, can I do Airbnb?” You have to sell the idea, show them the benefits and make it an easy yes. You might message 10 landlords and get only 1 yes, but 1 yes is all you need.

Pitch it as coliving

Leave out “Airbnb”

For many owners it means parties, noise and wear and tear.

Say “coliving”

Verified guests, rent guaranteed, the home professionally looked after. Coliving is growing, and owners of big apartments love it.

Where the profit is: we rent out every bedroom individually. Together the rooms bring in much more than the rent for the whole apartment.

Who you’re actually pitching to

Think about who rents out a second home. Often it’s a business owner or someone who has done well financially. People like that are often more open-minded about a business idea, and they understand the value of someone who runs things professionally.

The first apartment is the hardest. In Barcelona, many owners have several apartments, sometimes a whole building. We started with one, built trust, and then rented another apartment from the same owner. After the first yes it gets easier, also because you have proof to show.

Before you pitch: two case studies

What you pitch matters as much as how you pitch it. If you email every one- and two-bedroom flat on the market, you’ll hear “no” over and over, because those are exactly the places a landlord can rent to anyone. The fastest yes comes from the property the landlord struggles to rent. Here are two real cases from our own business, in two very different markets, so you know what to look for before you send a single email.

Case study · EuropeBarcelona: big apartments, rented room by room

Why landlords say yes here

In Barcelona, what works best for us are big apartments with 4 to 6 bedrooms. The historic centre is full of them, and owners find them hard to rent out:

  • The rent is often too high for a couple.
  • The people who are interested are often the wrong tenants. Usually it’s a group of young people. Many of them would sublet the rooms anyway, illegally, and some throw parties. That’s exactly what the owner is afraid of.
  • Families rarely live there. They usually don’t want to live in the busy, touristic centre.
  • They usually come unfurnished, so they can sit empty for months.

That’s your opening. You do the same thing those tenants would do, but legally, professionally and with everything organised and under control. You rent the whole apartment, furnish it, give it a fresh coat of paint, and rent out the rooms one by one: as coliving or mid-term stays, or short-term where the law allows it. The owner gets the entire apartment rented on one contract, rent on time, and a home that is painted and maintained far more often than with a normal tenant.

Our example: from 4 to 6 bedrooms

One of our latest apartments, very central, had 4 bedrooms and a huge living room. We added 2 bedrooms with one simple wall and an extra shower room, and it became our most profitable apartment. See the full story, with before and after photos, in Lesson 3.

What to look for in Europe if you want to do coliving

  • 4 to 6 bedrooms, at least 3, so you have enough rooms to rent out individually.
  • The numbers room by room. You’ll rent out each bedroom individually, like coliving, so divide the monthly rent by the number of bedrooms and compare that with what one room rents for in the area.
  • Furnished or unfurnished: an empty apartment means a furniture budget, but often a cheaper rent and a more motivated owner.
  • Enough bathrooms for the number of rooms, or space to add one.
  • Wasted space, like an oversized living room, that can become an extra bedroom.
Case study · AsiaBali: much easier to get a yes

A completely different market

In Bali, renting a property and subletting it legally is very common, so you don’t need much convincing, as long as your company and paperwork are in order. The number of bedrooms matters much less too: one to four bedrooms can all work, as long as the rent makes sense for the return you can get.

The catch: you pay much more up front. In Bali you don’t rent a place month to month.

How it works: leasehold

Most properties are rented on a leasehold: you pay for a fixed number of years in one go, often 25. When the lease ends, the property goes back to the owner, together with everything you built or improved on it.

You can also find leases for fewer years. We first took Casa Mewali (our small boutique villa, where we also rent out the rooms individually) for 3 years, with the right to extend written into the contract. Because you’re not paying the price of buying a property, it was still very affordable.

Why we chose Casa Mewali: built for coliving

We chose Casa Mewali because its setup is perfect for our coliving model: a shared pool with individual bedrooms around it. Instead of trying to rent out the entire villa, we divide it up and rent out the bedrooms one by one.

Casa Mewali, our small boutique villa in Bali.

Why rooms and not the whole villa? Most hosts in Bali rent out the entire villa, so that’s where the competition is. But a lot of travellers, many of them girls who love taking beautiful pictures, dream of staying in a villa this pretty and can’t afford the whole place. A single bedroom they can afford. That’s why people love booking this one.

Downstairs, 2 bedrooms open onto the pool, each with its own bathroom. Upstairs there is a third bedroom, also with its own bathroom. So: 3 suites around the pool, with the kitchen separate at the entrance. That lets us run 4 listings for one property: one for each room and one for the entire villa (the “List both ways” format from Lesson 1). Surprisingly, the entire villa has been booked only once. Almost every booking is for the rooms separately.

Not every property works like this. We have another property with 2 bedrooms whose architecture is much more family-style and private, so it’s not a great fit for strangers sharing it. For coliving, the layout decides.

What to look for in Bali

  • A rent that fits your numbers, whatever the number of bedrooms.
  • At least 3 bedrooms if you want to rent room by room.
  • A private bathroom for every bedroom.
  • Bedrooms that don’t open into each other, with shared spaces like the pool and kitchen apart from where people sleep.

Know your market before you pitch. In Europe, go for the big apartments landlords struggle to fill. In Bali, it’s much easier to get a yes, and with leasehold you can start with a short contract; for coliving, choose a layout with private bedrooms around shared spaces. Pitch the right property and you’ll hear yes much sooner, instead of collecting dozens of no’s and giving up.

Section 2

Handling objections

You found a great property. You pitch. The landlord isn’t convinced… yet.

Don’t freeze here. Objections are just questions in disguise. Understand the worry behind them and you can turn hesitation into a yes.

Common objections (and how to respond)

Tap an objection to see how to respond. Say your answer out loud before you open it. These are also your cheat sheet for the conversation.

“Isn’t subletting illegal?”

Not if it’s in the contract. Explain that they give you written permission to sublet in the rental contract, so everything is official. You follow the local rules (for example by offering mid-term stays of 31+ nights where short stays need a license) and you manage everything professionally: respectful guests, cleaning and noise control.

“What if guests damage the apartment?”

Explain that you’ll take out rental insurance and that you work with a professional handyman who fixes anything quickly. You only accept ID-verified guests, and you keep the apartment in excellent condition at all times, simply because you need great reviews to keep it booked. Damage is rare, and if something happens, you handle it. The owner won’t be bothered.

“I don’t want parties or problems.”

Tell them about your strict guest screening, house rules, and no-party policy. You use smart tools like noise monitors and security deposits to prevent issues.

“I don’t want random people in my property.”

Totally understandable. All guests are ID-verified, and they’re not party travelers: they’re often professionals staying for work or longer visits. You have strict house rules and you’re always reachable if anything comes up.

“I prefer a long-term tenant.”

You give them the same stable income, with more care for the property. The rent is guaranteed and on time, and if they ever want to go back to a traditional tenant, you handle the transition.

“Will this upset the neighbors?”

You screen every guest, enforce quiet hours and respectful behavior, and there’s always a local contact for emergencies and a direct line of communication.

“Why don’t you just rent it normally?”

Because this is a business, not a side hustle. Explain how your model gives the landlord stable rent, while you handle all the headaches of guest turnover, cleaning, and communication.

You can also show them what they gain compared with a classic long-term contract, where they are tied to the same tenant for years. With this model they keep flexibility: they don’t have to wait for a long contract to end to get their property back. If they have an emergency or simply need the property, they can ask for it back with a much shorter notice period. And on top of that, you take out rental insurance.

Extra card to playOffer to improve the apartment yourself

If you find an apartment with real potential, here is one more card you can play: offer to make some improvements at your own cost. For the same rent, the landlord gets a better apartment. That can be exactly what turns a “maybe” into a “yes”.

Our example

In one of our apartments, we replaced the old floor and turned the bathtub into a shower, which is also much easier for regular cleaning. The floor looked very old, and just changing it gave the whole apartment a makeover. Because the apartment looked so much better, we could rent the rooms at our prices and earn more.

Why it can make sense

You’re taking this apartment as an investment, so you already have a budget for setting it up. Include the cost of the improvements in that budget and in your profit calculator, and check that the higher prices you can ask pay it back.

How to use it

  • Ask first. Maybe the landlord is willing to do or pay for the work. It’s a negotiation, so start there.
  • Keep it as a card to play when the landlord hesitates, not as your opening offer.
  • Only if the numbers work. The improvement has to pay for itself within your contract.
  • Agree everything in writing: what you change, who pays, and what stays in the apartment when you leave.
Section 3

Bonus: scripts, email templates & face-to-face pitch

To help you confidently reach out to landlords, we’ve included a set of ready-to-use scripts, email templates, and face-to-face pitch outlines. These are based on real conversations that worked for us and are designed to position your offer in a professional, trustworthy way, even if you’re just starting out.

Whether you’re writing your first cold email or sitting down for a meeting, these templates will help you speak with clarity, build trust, and show landlords that you’re serious, prepared, and easy to work with. Just tweak the details to fit your situation and start pitching with confidence.

Fill in your details below once. They’re added to every template automatically, so you can copy and paste them straight away.

01 · EmailCold email to a landlord (initial contact)
Cold email to a landlord
Subject: Your rental property Hi , I saw your property and I'm interested in renting it. I run a small property management company, and I'd love to tell you more about how we work. Would you be open to a quick call or meeting this week? Best regards,
02 · In personFace-to-face pitch framework (landlord meeting)
Face-to-face pitch framework
Start with rapport: "Thanks for taking the time to meet. I'd like to explain a rental arrangement that could work well for both of us." Position the offer: "I run a small property rental business. I rent properties and host for stays. All our guests are ID-verified." Why it's easier than a normal tenant: "You get guaranteed payment: the rent is on time, every month. We work with a professional cleaner and handyman, so the place is always kept in excellent condition. No late payments, no chasing tenants, and no hidden damage at the end of a contract." Good communication: "You'll have one point of contact: me. I'll keep you updated and I'm always easy to reach." Close confidently: "Would you be open to giving this a try? We can put everything in a clear written agreement."
03 · EmailFollow-up email after a conversation
Follow-up email after a conversation
Subject: Follow-up on our conversation Hi , Thanks again for taking the time to chat. I know this approach may be different from a standard long-term rental, so I'd like to highlight the key benefits for you, especially compared with the typical risks landlords face. With a standard rental, it's common to experience things like: - Tenants who don't pay rent on time or stop paying altogether - Properties left in poor condition after move-out - Difficulties accessing the property for inspections or maintenance - Disputes over damage, deposits or responsibility for upkeep What we offer is a hands-off, professional arrangement that protects your property and gives you peace of mind: Monthly rent: , guaranteed and on time, every month Guests: ID-verified Cleaning: Professionally cleaned, far more often than with a standard tenant Maintenance: Regularly inspected and maintained by our professional handyman, at no cost to you I'll attach our information brochure about rental arbitrage, so you can see exactly how it works. Let me know if you have any questions. I'm happy to explain anything in more detail. Looking forward to hearing your thoughts,
Open the PDF in Google Drive
Customizable

Landlord information brochure

Use this PDF to introduce yourself to landlords and help them understand exactly what you do and how your rental model works. Attaching this PDF to your email increases your chances, because it looks professional and clearly presents your idea.

Access your template

Opens the editable design in Canva, where you add your own name, photos and numbers.

Section 4

Closing the deal

Pro tips for closing the deal

  • Speak their language. Don’t sell the dream of hosting. Sell peace of mind. Focus on how you’ll take care of their property, pay rent on time, and be the best tenant they’ve ever had.
  • Use social proof. Show examples of your listings, reviews or experience. If you’re new, share what you’ve learned and your plan. Confidence builds trust.
  • Show that you know the rules. Explain exactly what’s allowed in their area (for example mid-term stays of 31+ nights) and how you’ll follow it. Owners relax when they see you’ve done your homework.
  • Show your systems. Bring the tools from this course: your property manual, cleaning and inspection checklists, contracts for your team and your house rules. It shows you run this professionally.
  • Offer a win-win. Think about what the landlord wants most: no stress, steady income, a well-kept property. Your offer should check those boxes clearly.
  • Know your stuff. The more confident you are, and the better you know the official rules and how everything works, the more owners will trust you.
  • Always get it in writing. Once they say yes, have a simple agreement ready to sign. It protects both sides and shows you’re serious.

Put it in writing

A yes only counts once it’s on paper. What needs to be in writing depends on your business model:

Rental arbitrage: add a subletting clause to your rental contract. Your contract must clearly say that you’re allowed to sublet the property. Without that clause, subletting isn’t permitted, even if the owner agreed in person. You can use this as a starting point:

“The landlord authorizes the tenant to sublet the property, in whole or in part, to third parties for short-term and mid-term stays, and to advertise it on online rental platforms. The tenant remains fully responsible for paying the rent and for the condition of the property.”

Ask a local lawyer or your rental agency to check the wording, because contract rules are different in every country.

  • Co-hosting: you don’t sign a rental contract. Instead, sign a co-hosting agreement with the owner that covers your tasks, your commission, who pays for what, and how either of you can end it.
  • Buying a property: you don’t need anyone’s permission to rent it out, but check the building or homeowners’ association rules and the local license rules before you complete the purchase.

Final Word

You’re not begging for permission. You’re offering a professional service. Be respectful, but firm. Be clear, but flexible. You’ll hear plenty of no’s, but with the right pitch and the right attitude, you will get that yes.

Now go close the deal!

Part 2 · Lesson 7

Set up a space that books itself

What to buy, how to design it, how to guest-proof it.

4 sections · about 15 minLesson07
Section 1

What you really need

(and what’s a waste of money)

When you’re setting up your first property, it’s tempting to think you need to buy everything. But most of that is just noise. What really matters is creating a space that’s comfortable, functional, and stands out without blowing your budget.

✓ Essentials

What you really need

  • A comfortable bed with good-quality bedding
  • Blackout curtains so guests can sleep well
  • Free earplugs if noise could be an issue
  • Strong Wi-Fi (non-negotiable)
  • A clean, functional kitchen or kitchenette
  • A smooth, stress-free self-check-in
  • A full-length mirror (very important for female guests), hooks, hair dryer, hangers, towels, soap and toilet paper
  • A simple system for cleaning, restocking and guest communication
✕ Skip it

What’s a waste of money

  • Designer brands no one notices
  • Huge TVs in every room
  • Welcome baskets that aren’t consistent or scalable
  • Expensive tech or “smart home” extras you don’t need
  • Overbuying before you know what guests care about
Start simple, but start smart. The essentials are your non-negotiable foundation. They make the place feel like home. Prioritize comfort, flow and design, and build from there.
Example · long-term staysA bedroom that has everything a guest needs

One of the bedrooms in our long-term apartments in Barcelona.

A simple setup, but it has everything a guest needs to feel at home. That matters more than expensive furniture.

  • A board for photos. A cheap felt “cloud” from Temu. Long-term guests love to put up photos, and this way they don’t stain your walls.
  • A storage bed that lifts up, for suitcases and extra storage.
  • A simple open clothes rack, no fancy wardrobe.
  • A desk and chair, a bedside lamp and curtains: good lighting and curtains make a big difference.
  • A good lock on the inside and outside of the door.
  • A framed welcome page and a laundry basket.

Don’t overcomplicate it with expensive or crazy furniture. It’s the small details, like a laundry basket and a place for photos, that get you 5-star reviews, because guests can see an experienced host set this up.

A chain lock on the inside, a hook for the room key, and a holder for the AC remote with a short label.

Section 2

Design a space that fully books

(even on a budget)

In competitive markets, guests scroll fast. If your place doesn’t pop, it gets skipped. You don’t need expensive furniture or a stylist. You need a consistent look and good lighting.

+20–30%A well-designed space can increase your nightly rate by 20–30% and keep you booked, even in low season.
1

Choose a clear style

Boho, minimalist, modern, industrial. Pick one and stay consistent, so the space feels intentional.

2

Stick to a color palette

Use 2–3 main colors (neutrals + one accent) for a calm, organized look.

3

Add 1–2 statement pieces

A bold headboard, unique lighting, a large mirror or a piece of art. That’s your wow factor.

4

Use textiles for warmth

Throws, rugs, curtains and pillows make a space cozy and layered, even with basic furniture.

5

Lighting is everything

Warm bulbs, several light sources (not just the ceiling light) and a few lamps create a cozy glow. Good lighting makes your photos look 10x better.

Even with a minimal budget, you can create a space that feels elevated. And that’s what gets clicks, bookings and five-star reviews.

Design is what sets you apart

Same villa, same pool, same walls. Paint, gravel, curtains and a few clay pots turned a plain place into one guests choose on sight.

Guests happily pay more for a space that feels beautiful and ready from the moment they arrive. Even in a saturated market like Bali, that is what turns a regular listing into a profitable one. Lesson 7 shows you what to buy and what is a waste of money.

A beautiful design can earn you 20–30% more, and we teach you how to get there without spending a fortune.

See before/after on Instagram
Section 3

Guest-proof your space

Here’s the truth: things will break, guests will test your systems, and the more you grow, the more moving parts you’ll have. You want a place that runs like a well-oiled machine, even when you’re on the other side of the world.

1

Choose durable over delicate

Skip fragile items and high-maintenance fabrics. Go for:

  • Washable, stain-resistant bedding (beige hides stains better than white)
  • Easy-to-clean furniture and rugs (get a couch cover)
  • Hard-to-break plates and glasses (wine glasses break easily)
  • Wall-mounted lamps or nightstands
  • Scratch-resistant stainless steel pans
2

Think like a cleaner

“How quickly can this place be reset for the next guest?”

  • Minimal decor, so surfaces are easy to wipe
  • No open shelves that collect dust
  • Backup supplies in a locked cabinet
  • Labeled baskets for towels, sheets and essentials

If your cleaner finishes without messaging you, you’re winning.

3

Anchor everything

Secure furniture to the wall, especially in family-friendly units. Tape down rug corners, use non-slip pads and avoid anything that tips easily.

4

Keep it simple for guests

  • Signs or frames that show how appliances work
  • A clear house manual
  • Automated check-in and check-out instructions
  • Wi-Fi codes and emergency info somewhere obvious

Fewer questions = fewer headaches.

5

Lock up what’s off-limits

Keep a locked owner’s closet for tools, backup stock and valuables. If you don’t want it touched, don’t leave it out.

6

Bonus: smart setups

  • Key boxes or smart locks, so there are no key handovers
  • Motion-sensor lights in hallways or outdoors
  • Labels on drawers and cabinets
Set it up once. A resilient, guest-friendly space saves you hours in daily operations and protects your profit in the long run.
Section 4

Bonus: full setup checklist

This checklist is designed for a standard one-bedroom apartment that sleeps two guests. You can easily adjust it based on your space and needs.

Important: always keep your welcome materials looking clean and professional. Torn, dirty, or messy booklets leave a bad impression. It's better to have none than to leave out one that looks neglected.

Part 2 · Lesson 8

Create a listing that sells

Even while you sleep.

7 sections · about 40 minLesson08
Section 1

Before you go live

Your listing is almost ready to go online. Before your first guest pays you, make sure the paperwork is in place. You chose your setup in Lesson 2; now it’s time to make it official. Renting out as a private individual? Then you can skip the registration, but still keep track of your income so you can declare it.

Your tasks
Section 2

Your first listing

It’s time to create your first listing. Airbnb is our favorite platform, and it’s where we recommend you start.

Create your first Airbnb listing

*This is an affiliate link. No worries: creating your listing through it costs you nothing extra, we simply receive a commission. Thank you for your support!
P.S. Once you’re set up, you can get your own link too and earn by referring other hosts to Airbnb.

Good to know

Which platform should you use?

Airbnb is the most used platform in most of the world, and the easiest one to set up and manage. For years, it was the only one we used. But in some regions, like parts of Asia, many guests book on Booking.com, even if it’s less user-friendly. So check which platforms are popular in your area before you decide. Starting on Airbnb? Use our link to create your listing*.

You can also list on several platforms at once. Just connect your calendars, so you never get a double booking. A channel manager like Lodgify does this for you and keeps all your messages in one place.

Platforms:AirbnbBooking.comVrbo
Your tasks
Section 3

Write a title and description that convert

Your title and description are your first (and sometimes only) chance to grab attention and turn a scroll into a booking. This is your mini sales pitch. It needs to stand out, spark curiosity, and communicate value in just a few seconds.

Start with a scroll-stopping title

Think of your title as your headline. It’s what makes people stop and click. You only get 50 characters, so every word counts.

What works:

  • Highlight a standout feature (rooftop, pool, view, design)
  • Mention who it’s ideal for (couples, remote workers, families)
  • Use emotional words or paint a picture (“Peaceful jungle retreat” vs. “Private room in Ubud”)

Examples:

  • "Boho Loft with Rooftop Views in Central Barcelona"
  • "Romantic Jungle Hideaway with Private Pool"
  • "Stylish Flat 5 min from the Beach + Free Bikes"
From our own listings

Tap a listing to see it live.

Why it works: Leads with the view guests want and is honest that it’s a shared villa. Guests can already imagine themselves lying in bed, looking out at the pool.View listingWhy it works: A tiny room without windows, and still one of our most requested rooms. People love to stay in a big shared apartment with balconies, even on a lower budget.View listingWhy it works: It highlights the best feature of the apartment: the huge private rooftop. One word in capitals adds emphasis, and the location does the rest.View listing
Your listing details (fill in once, used in both prompts)
AI prompt: generate a scroll-stopping title

Copy and open in:ChatGPTGeminiClaude

Your description = your story

Once they click, your description should guide the guest through the experience of staying at your place. Think of it as a conversation, not a brochure.

Break it into short sections to make it easy to skim:

The Space: Describe the vibe, layout, and highlights. Help them imagine being there.

The Experience: What makes your place special? What can they expect? Is it peaceful? Lively? Designed for productivity? Tailor this to your audience.

The Location: Add what’s nearby (cafés, sights, walkability) to make it feel like they’re already there.

Essentials: Mention anything that stands out: fast WiFi, free parking, filtered water, daily cleaning, fully equipped kitchen, etc.

Bonus Tip: Use formatting to your advantage. Short sentences, bullet points, and line breaks help your listing stand out.

A great title gets the click. A great description closes the deal.
