Your tasks
Section 4

Take quality photos without hiring a pro

You don’t need to spend hundreds on a professional photographer to create a high-converting listing. With the right approach, you can take stunning photos yourself, even with a smartphone. The key is understanding what guests want to see and how to showcase your space in the best possible light.

Clean and stage your space

Before taking any pictures, make sure everything is spotless and styled. Open the curtains, fluff the pillows, and hide cords, visible bins and remotes. The photos must show the place as it really is, but you can remove items that make it look cluttered. Think of it like setting the stage; you want it to look welcoming, calm, and inviting.

Lighting is everything

Natural light is your best friend. Shoot during the day when your space is the brightest, ideally in the morning or late afternoon. Turn off overhead lights to avoid yellow tones. Open windows and let daylight in.

Use a good phone or camera

Most modern smartphones are more than enough. Just make sure your lens is clean and the resolution is set to high quality. Avoid using filters or heavy editing. Guests want to see the real space.

Shoot horizontally

Always take photos in landscape mode (horizontal), not vertical. Airbnb displays your listing photos in landscape, so this format gives a better view of each space.

Capture wide angles

Stand in corners or doorways to get as much of the room in the shot as possible. Use a wide-angle setting if available, but don’t distort the room. Guests want a real sense of space, not a fisheye view. On an iPhone Pro, the 0.5 lens works best.

Include every important area

Show everything: entryway, closets, appliances, amenities, parking, balcony, views. If it adds value, capture it. Lack of transparency leads to bad reviews.

Your photo order matters (this is crucial for bookings).

Your first picture is your million-dollar shot. It’s what sells your listing, and it matters more than anything else: it’s what brings in the clicks, the bookings and the income. Use your most eye-catching image as cover photo. Bedrooms usually perform best. Follow up with 4 key shots of different rooms that highlight your space’s best features. Airbnb shows only the first 5 photos before guests have to click “Show all photos,” so this is where you make a strong first impression and grab their attention.

Check out our listing as an example

Real life example

Sometimes the smallest details make the biggest difference. In one of our Barcelona apartments, we had two identical rooms; same size, same layout, just mirrored. Yet one was always fully booked, while the other struggled to get reservations unless we dropped the price.

The only difference? The desk.

Visually, the desk in the popular room made the space look bigger and more inviting. That slight design edge translated into significantly better performance and higher profit. We swapped out the less appealing desk, and suddenly both rooms booked out at full price.

The takeaway: If your bookings are slow, take a hard look at your listing. Tiny design choices can cost you money.

Highlight the experience

Instead of just showing rooms, capture little moments such as a cup on the coffee table, cozy blankets, books on a nightstand. It makes guests imagine themselves staying there.

Photos are the most important part of your listing. This is where you sell your space before guests read the description. A great listing with bad photos won’t get bookings. But even a simple space with beautiful, clear, well-lit images can perform incredibly well.

So if photography isn’t your strength, consider asking a friend with a good eye or hiring someone locally. It’s a small investment that can pay off big.

Your tasks
Section 5

Important listing details that protect you

This section can save you from headaches, bad reviews, and refund requests.

Your listing description isn’t just a sales pitch. It’s also your legal shield. Whatever you clearly mention in writing can protect you from guest complaints, refund requests, and bad reviews.

So don’t hold back. Be honest, be detailed, and include everything that could potentially become a problem.

Here’s what to include: House rules: Be clear and specific. No smoking? Quiet hours? Visitors allowed? Extra fee for late check-in? Spell it all out. Don’t assume people will “just know.”

Special things to note:

Is there potential for noise from nearby bars? Are there stairs, shared spaces, or pets on the property? Mention them all.

Shared Spaces:

If your listing is not fully private, you need to state this clearly and more than once. Even if it’s already mentioned in the listing, repeat it in the description. Put it in CAPITALS. Make it obvious. Some guests will still “miss it” and claim they didn’t know. If it’s written clearly, Airbnb will side with you.

Safety & Boundaries

Include a statement like: "In case of disrespectful, aggressive, or intoxicated behavior, the host reserves the right to cancel the reservation without refund to protect the property and maintain a safe environment.”

It might feel like you’re being overly cautious, but trust us: you’re not. You’re protecting your peace and your business.

The more transparent you are, the fewer problems you’ll have. Take time to list everything that matters.

Copy/paste our house rules

Guests accept your house rules before booking, so they protect you as a host. But Airbnb has new rules for this. For bookings made from 20 November 2026, your house rules must be in the house rules section of your listing before guests book. You can’t add new rules later by message, with signs in the home or in person.

Your rules must also be reasonable. That means no fines or penalties, no extra fees for things that are part of your listing, and no chores a cleaner would normally do, like washing dishes, stripping the bed or taking the trash out of the building. Small requests, like putting used dishes in the sink, are still fine. Keep your rules short and clear: guests actually read them that way.

House rules: private property

House rules: shared property
Change the parts in [brackets], then copy into the house rules section of your listing. Saved on this device.
Your tasks
Section 6

Pricing strategies

to stay competitive from day one

Setting the right price is one of the most important factors for your success, especially when you're just getting started. If your price is too high, your listing won’t get traction. Too low, and you might fill your calendar but leave money on the table.

Here’s how to price smart from day one:

Start lower to build momentum

When your listing is new and doesn’t have reviews yet, guests are taking a small risk by booking. To overcome that, offer a competitive introductory price (10–20% below market average). This helps you get your first few bookings and collect 5-star reviews faster which boosts your search ranking.

Use dynamic pricing tools

Tools like PriceLabs, Wheelhouse, or Airbnb’s Smart Pricing adjust your nightly rate based on demand, seasonality, events, and competitor pricing. These tools help you avoid undercharging on busy weekends or high seasons.

Pro tip: Airbnb’s Smart Pricing tends to undervalue your listing. Use it with caution and always set a minimum price you’re comfortable with.

Research competitors

Research similar listings in your area. Look at:

  • Their nightly rate
  • Cleaning fees
  • Availability
  • Amenities offered
  • Reviews

If they’re booked out and you’re not, it’s likely a pricing (or photo) issue. Adjust accordingly.

Offer weekly & monthly discounts

To encourage longer stays and fill your calendar, set smart discounts for weekly and monthly bookings. This can help increase occupancy and reduce turnover work, especially during slower seasons.

Don’t rely on just the nightly rate

Your cleaning fee and minimum stay also impact how attractive your listing is. If your cleaning fee is too high compared to your nightly rate, it might drive guests away, especially for short stays.

Raise your price strategically

Once you have at least 5 strong reviews and some social proof, you can gradually increase your prices. Don’t make a big jump overnight; test small increases and monitor your bookings.

Use discounts the right way

Airbnb offers tools like “early bird” discounts, “last-minute” discounts, and promotions for new listings. Use them strategically to stay booked without cheapening your brand.

Final note

Pricing is never “set it and forget it.” Revisit your strategy every week or two, especially in the beginning. Stay flexible, use data, and optimize based on results, not just assumptions.

With the right pricing strategy, you can stay competitive, attract quality guests, and build up your income from the very first listing.

Part 2 · Lesson 9

Deliver an unforgettable guest experience for 5-star reviews

Expectations, complaints and great service.

4 sections · about 30 minLesson09
Section 1

Setting expectations early

Setting clear expectations upfront is one of the most effective ways to avoid misunderstandings, prevent complaints, and ensure a smooth experience for both you and your guests.

Before a guest even books, your listing should clearly communicate exactly what they’re getting. This includes things like:

  • Whether the space is private or shared
  • Quiet hours and noise potential
  • Rules about visitors, smoking, or pets
  • Layout of the space and shared areas
  • Location details (e.g., if it’s in a lively area or a quiet neighborhood)
  • Any limitations or quirks (e.g., steep stairs, construction nearby, no elevator)

It might feel like you’re pointing out negatives, but transparency builds trust. It also protects you. If issues come up, you can always point back to what was clearly mentioned before booking.

Here’s where you should reinforce expectations:

  • Your listing description and house rules
  • The welcome message right after booking
  • Signage or reminders in the property (when necessary)

It’s okay to repeat the same things several times, especially if guests share common spaces.

Being honest doesn’t scare good guests away. It filters out the ones who aren’t the right fit, and those are often the ones who create problems. Setting expectations early makes your life easier, your reviews better, and your hosting stress-free.

How to make guests follow your rules: make them clear
  1. Write rules that are specific. “Check-out is strictly at 11:00 AM” works. “Please be respectful” does not.
  2. Put them in your house rules. Guests have to accept them before booking, so you can always refer back to them.
  3. Repeat them. In the listing description, in the welcome message, and on signs or labels inside the property.
  4. Keep them short. Guests are tired when traveling and ignore long texts.
  5. Be polite but firm when a rule is broken. Point to the rule they agreed to.

Example: shared spaces

We mention in our listing seven times that the kitchen and pool are shared, plus one final reminder in the welcome message. And still, occasionally, a guest arrives claiming we didn't mention it and asks for a full refund.

The reality is: some people simply don’t read. But that’s their responsibility, not yours. As long as you’ve clearly stated it in multiple places, you’re fully protected. If you can prove it was communicated upfront, guests will accept that they made a mistake, and Airbnb will side with you.

Example: construction noise

If something could affect the guest experience, like construction noise nearby, frame it as a benefit rather than a problem. For example, mention in your listing that the current rate already includes a special discount due to temporary construction in the area.

This way, guests feel like they’re getting a deal. Often, you don’t even need to reduce your price significantly. Just highlighting that a discount has been applied makes guests think, “I’m getting a great offer,” rather than focusing on the inconvenience. It's all about how you position it.

Section 2

How to handle complaints or damages

No matter how well you prepare, at some point some guests will complain or cause damage. What separates great hosts from the rest is how they respond.

1

Stay calm and respond fast

Reply quickly and professionally, even if the complaint feels unfair or minor. Acknowledge the issue, thank the guest for letting you know, and tell them you’re working on a solution.

YouThank you for sharing this with us. We’re so sorry for the inconvenience and we will do our best to find a solution.
2

Evaluate and take action

Minor complaintOffer a solution quickly: send the cleaner again, give a small refund or replace what’s missing.
Bigger issueGather evidence first: security footage, message logs, cleaner reports, or a visit if you’re nearby.
3

Document everything, especially with photos

Keep screenshots, pictures and receipts. If there’s damage, take clear photos and file a damage claim through Airbnb within 14 days or before the next guest checks in, whichever comes first.

Important: ask your cleaner to always take photos if something is damaged or missing (even towels). A quick photo of the room before and after each turnover can be your best proof in a dispute.
4

Be firm when needed

If a guest breaks a house rule or causes damage, be polite but direct. Point to the listing and house rules they agreed to when booking.

YouAs stated in the house rules, parties are not allowed. Due to the disturbance and cleanup required, we’ll need to charge an additional fee to cover the extra cleaning and guest compensation.
5

Don’t take it personally

Not every review will be 5 stars, and not every guest will behave perfectly. Learn from each case, improve your systems and keep going. Over time you’ll face fewer problems.

You never know what someone is going through. Traveling makes people tired, anxious or irritable. Arguing, even when you’re completely right, rarely ends well.

Our golden rule

Kill them with kindness. Acknowledge their experience, show understanding and tell them you’ll do your best to help. This simple shift in tone can calm a tense situation and turn a potential conflict into a positive review.

Handling complaints or damages is part of the business. The faster and more professionally you respond, the better your reviews and your peace of mind.

Dealing with a difficult guest? We have a dedicated lesson: Difficult guests.

Something big broke? Read our bonus lesson Damage & AirCover: what to do, and how to get reimbursed.

At the end of this lesson, you’ll get access to a ready-to-use 'Quick Replies Library' with message templates to handle common issues. You can copy and paste them directly to save time and respond professionally in any situation.

Section 3

How to be a 5-star host

Being a 5-star host doesn’t mean being available 24/7 or bending over backward for every request. It means creating a seamless, thoughtful experience before, during and after the stay. Great service is often what separates a 4-star review from a 5-star one.

Before check-in

Proactive communication

  • Send a warm, clear pre-arrival message: address, check-in time, how to get there and how to get in (see the bonus templates)
  • Ask for their arrival time and any special needs
  • Answer questions before they ask: Wi-Fi, local tips, what to expect
  • Be friendly but professional. You’re setting the tone.
During the stay

Available, not intrusive

  • Check in after the first night. A simple “Hope everything’s going well! Let me know if you need anything” goes a long way.
  • Make sure your welcome booklet or digital guide answers the FAQs
  • If a problem comes up, respond fast and keep the guest informed, even if you can’t fix it right away
After check-out

Leave a lasting impression

  • Thank them for staying and invite them to leave a review
  • If you solved a problem, mention it: “Thanks again for your patience with the plumbing issue, we’re glad we could sort it quickly!”
★★★★★
The cherry on top

Tell them you’re leaving them 5 stars

Most guests simply check out and never leave a review. A short message after check-out changes that. When you tell guests they were great and that you’re leaving them a 5-star review, they’re much more likely to review you back, and to give you 5 stars too.

YouThank you so much for staying with us! You were amazing guests, and we’ve just left you a 5-star review. If you enjoyed your stay, we’d be so grateful if you left us one too. Safe travels!
Be humanA warm tone beats robotic professionalism.
Be clearClear instructions and expectations reduce stress.
Be honestIf something goes wrong, own it and offer a solution.
Be kindEspecially with complaints, empathy always wins.

Customer service isn’t just about fixing problems. It’s about showing guests you care. When they feel cared for, they leave happier, review better and recommend your place.

Section 4

Bonus: 'quick replies' library

Here’s your ready-to-use library of quick replies for guest communication. These messages are designed to save you time, deliver consistent service, and handle common questions with ease. You can personalize them by filling in the blanks and manually adding each one into the Airbnb app.

Great communication = great reviews.

How to use the library
  • Where they go: if you use Airbnb, you can add them manually in the app, under “Quick replies”. You add each one by hand once. It takes a bit of effort upfront, but it saves you hours in the long run.
  • Automatic or not: quick replies are not automatic. You pick one and send it when a guest asks. The messages that go out on their own are the five scheduled messages in Lesson 12.

Part 3 · Lesson 10

You’re not doing this alone. Build your dream team

Agency or own team, and how to find reliable people.

4 sections · about 20 minLesson10
Section 1

Hiring an agency or creating your own team

We personally started by doing everything ourselves, not because we wanted to, but because we didn’t have the budget for a team in the beginning. And honestly, it was one of the best ways to learn the business inside out. But let’s be real: cleaning toilets and fixing light bulbs isn’t what grows your business.

While it’s helpful to understand how every part works, the manager role is by far the most important. That’s the person who keeps operations running, guests happy, and problems solved.

Our recommendation: start small but strategic. Begin by hiring one cleaner (and make sure you also have a backup option), and find a reliable freelance handyman who can handle basic maintenance. You don’t have to hire them officially. If you rent out as a private individual or as self-employed, you can work with them as freelancers. Just put your agreement in writing: that’s always better for both sides.

Then, for the first few weeks, manage the listing yourself. Respond to guests, handle check-ins, deal with minor issues, and file damage requests with Airbnb.

This will teach you the platform, the guest journey, and the kinds of things that actually come up.

Once that’s running smoothly and you know what the job involves, you’ll be in a much better position to hire a manager. You’ll understand how long tasks take, what tools they need, and what quality looks like.

Ideally, your manager should live near the property so they can also serve as the emergency contact, someone who can be on-site quickly if there’s ever an issue while you’re away.

This setup gives you the best of both worlds:

  • You keep profit margins high
  • You stay in control
  • You gradually remove yourself from daily tasks without losing oversight
Remember: you don’t need to work in your business. You want a business that works FOR you!

We personally prefer this approach over using an agency because it allows us to build our own team with people we trust and vibe with, while still making the business fully passive over time.

The best part? You stay in control. You set the systems, the standards, and the guest experience.

With an agency, you’re tied to their team, their tools, and their way of working which may not match your vision or priorities. That’s why if you’re considering going the agency route, it’s crucial to find one that aligns with your values and expectations.

It’s also worth running the numbers: compare what you’d spend paying your own team (cleaners, manager, handyman) vs. how much you’d lose by handing over 15–30% of your income to an agency.

You might find that keeping things in-house or semi-in-house gives you more freedom and more profit without sacrificing quality.

Overview

Doing it all yourself
→ don’t recommend0-10%passive income

You handle everything: cleaning, guest communication, maintenance, pricing, and restocking.

✓ Pros
  • Full control
  • Highest profit margins
  • Learn the business inside out
✕ Cons
  • Very time-consuming
  • No backup when you’re unavailable
  • Easy to burn out without systems

Best forSolo hosts just starting out, or anyone who wants full control and is managing 1–2 listings

Create a team, stay in control of high-level tasks
→ start here70-80%passive income

You manage high-level strategy while outsourcing tasks like cleaning, guest communication and maintenance.

✓ Pros
  • Best of both worlds
  • Highest profit margins
  • You stay in control
  • Reduces workload without full outsourcing
✕ Cons
  • Still requires oversight
  • You need to set up your own systems

Best forDetail-oriented and new hosts who want to stay in control and still do some of the work themselves.

Create your own team to manage everything
→ our favorite90%passive income

You hire part-time or full-time cleaners, handymen, and/or a manager/cohost.

✓ Pros
  • Higher profit margins
  • Full control of branding and experience
  • You choose who you work with
✕ Cons
  • Time-consuming to recruit & train
  • You need to set up your own systems

Best forDetail-oriented hosts with a growing portfolio and strong local presence.

Hiring an agency
→ if you want zero involvement90-100%passive income

You outsource everything to a property management agency.

✓ Pros
  • Hands-off management
  • Full peace of mind
  • Saves time
✕ Cons
  • 15%–30% of revenue
  • Less control over guest experience

Best forOwners who want 100% passive income or live far from the property

Your tasks
Section 2

Building your own team

When you’re launching your first listing, you can do things yourself. But if you plan to scale, you’ll want a small, reliable team. Build it in this order:

1
Hire first

A cleaner (and a backup)

Guests expect spotless spaces and tight turnovers. A good cleaner keeps your ratings high and saves you from doing all the dirty work. Always have a backup cleaner. Life happens, and you don’t want to be stuck when your main cleaner can’t make it.

Bonus tip: pay per checkout, not per hour. Every guest is different: some leave the place spotless, others leave a mess. In our shared apartments, we use a hybrid model: a fixed rate for the common areas, plus a fee per room cleaned.
Smart detail: a washing cycle takes about 1 hour and 15 minutes, so it naturally keeps the cleaner on-site long enough to finish the full turnover properly.
2
Next

A handyman

For small repairs, maintenance and unexpected fixes. You don’t need someone full-time, just a trustworthy person you can call when something breaks.

3
Once it runs smoothly

A manager or co-host

They handle day-to-day operations: guest messages, check-ins and coordinating the team. Hire someone who lives nearby, so they can also be your emergency contact and go to the property if needed. You can also find a co-host on Airbnb itself.

Do it yourself firstDo this role yourself for the first few weeks. Then you’ll know exactly what to delegate and what to expect.
Section 3

How to find reliable people

Hiring the right people can make or break your hosting business. A great team keeps everything running smoothly. The wrong people cost you time, money and 5-star reviews.

1

Ask other hosts

The best hires often come from word of mouth. Join local Facebook groups for hosts or expats in your area and ask for trusted contacts.

2

Start with a test job

Before giving someone full responsibility, try one small task, like a trial cleaning or a basic repair. Check their reliability, communication and attention to detail.

3

Be extremely clear

People can’t read your mind. Share exactly what you expect, how and when.

  • Use templates and checklists
  • Give access to your property wiki (see bonus template)
  • Put everything in writing and have them sign it (see the agreements below)
4

Pay on time, be kind

Reliable people stay when they’re treated well. Pay fairly and consistently, say thank you, and let them know they matter. Good relationships mean better work and longer partnerships.

5

Have a backup for every role

Even the best people get sick, go on holiday or move away. Always have at least one backup cleaner, handyman and emergency contact. It keeps your business running and gives you peace of mind.

Good to know: it’s completely normal to go through a few hires and fires before you find people who are reliable and fit your standards. Don’t get discouraged. It’s part of the process.
Section 4

Bonus: contract and agreement templates

These contract templates are designed for freelancers and independent contractors. They're not employment agreements, but rather clear outlines of responsibilities, payment terms, and expectations for roles like cleaners, manager, pool cleaner/gardener, handyman (optional)...

Use them to avoid misunderstandings, protect your business, and ensure everyone is on the same page from day one. You can easily customize them to fit your property setup and local regulations.

Part 3 · Lesson 11

Streamline your operations

Turnovers, supplies, SOPs, labels and inspections.

7 sections · about 30 minLesson11
Section 1

Workflows for turnovers and check-ins

Smooth turnovers and seamless check-ins are what separate amateur hosts from professional operators. If you want to scale or step away from daily management, you need systems that run without you. Turnovers and check-ins aren’t just chores: they’re your frontline guest experience, and your reviews (and revenue) will show it.

1

Create a turnover routine

Hotels clean in the same proven order every time. Steal that strategy: from how to enter the apartment to the order of the rooms, a set process means nothing gets missed and new team members learn fast.

Templates are waiting at the end of this lesson.

2

Same products, same place

If the towels are always in the same drawer and the coffee is always on the left shelf, your team works faster and guests don’t message you asking where things are. Keep backups in a labeled, locked space.

3

Rotate linens smartly

Have three sets of linens per bed and three sets of towels per guest, so you’re never caught off guard on quick turnovers:

1 in use1 clean & ready1 in the wash
4

A lost & found box

Keep a small box in a hidden but accessible spot for anything guests leave behind. Your cleaner puts forgotten items there. Empty it once a month: throw leftovers away or give them to the cleaner.

5

Have a backup plan

Cleaners get sick. Guests check in early. The internet goes down. Make sure you have:

  • A backup cleaner or co-host you can call
  • A process for emergency maintenance
  • Clear SOPs anyone can follow if you’re unavailable
6

Train once, delegate forever

Build a property wiki: one place where everything about your listing lives, from how to restock to what to do if the toilet leaks. Onboarding gets fast, and questions and errors drop.

Remember: The most important tasks are mapped out for you, in order, inside your bonus “Roadmap: task checklist to launch your first listing.” Use it as your step-by-step guide to stay on track and avoid missing anything important.

Section 2

Managing supplies and restocking

Behind the scenes, how you manage supplies and laundry can make or break the guest experience (and your sanity). The goal: no last-minute runs for toilet paper and no stress over missing sheets.

1

Set up a clear inventory system

List every essential, from toilet paper and soap to sponges, trash bags and coffee. Track how much is used per week or per guest, and set a minimum stock level. When you hit it, restock.

Pro tipLog usage and quantities in a Notion or Google Sheets tracker. You’ll find a template in the bonus resources.
2

Decide who restocks, and give them a working capital

Decide who buys the supplies (cleaner, manager or you), how often, and how you’ll reimburse them.

Working capital: a set monthly amount in cash or a digital wallet, so your team never pays out of pocket. Top it up monthly or whenever it runs low.
Stay on budgetKeep all receipts in a shared folder or Notion tracker. Even easier: a WhatsApp group where your team posts a photo of each receipt and the remaining balance.
Section 3

SOPs, task templates and property manual

to keep everything running smoothly

If you want your property to run like a well-oiled machine, especially when you’re not there, SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) are your secret weapon. They’re simply clear, written instructions for how things are done, so you never have to explain the same thing twice.

The SOPs you’ll want to set up

Cleaning checklistRoom-by-room tasks in order of priority
Turnover workflowWhat happens between checkout and the next guest
Guest check-inFrom automatic messages to key handovers or smart locks
Restocking & suppliesWhat needs to be in stock at all times
Reporting issuesWhat to do if something breaks or a guest complains
EmergenciesContacts, troubleshooting, water leaks, lost keys and so on
Maintenance scheduleMonthly or quarterly checks to avoid costly repairs
Put it all in one place

Your property manual. A shared Google Doc, a Notion page or a printed folder in the property, as long as your team can always find it. It’s one of the best time-saving systems you can create.

Open the property manual
Section 4

Labels and little details

Labels for clarity and consistency

Clear labels keep your team organized, confuse guests less and save time on every turnover.

✓ Everything goes back in the right place✓ New team members learn faster✓ More intuitive for guests✓ Less loss or misuse of supplies✓ Fewer daily questions
For guests

What to label

  • Fridge shelves (with room or suite names)
  • Kitchen cabinets and drawers (shared vs. private)
  • Water dispensers (“Drinking water only”)
  • Trash and recycling bins
  • The washing machine program you recommend
  • Bathroom storage (“Shared” / “Private”)
For your team

What to label

  • Cleaning product shelves or boxes
  • Restock bins (“Spare towels”, “Toilet paper stock”)
  • The lost & found box
  • Garden tools or pool supplies
  • Wash cycle instructions on the machine
  • Laundry baskets (“Dirty towels”, “Stained sheets”, “Ready to wash”)
Label tips: use laminated or waterproof labels in kitchens, bathrooms and outdoors. Add icons or color codes if your team speaks different languages (free icons at flaticon.com). Keep font, size and wording consistent, and a simple laminating machine or label maker for renewals. Keep it simple: “Suite 1 shelf”, “Refills only”, “Not for guests”. One language plus icons, never a wall of text.

Little details that save big headaches

Once your operations are running, it’s the tiny things no one thinks to document that cause the biggest slowdowns. These extra details save you hours of messages and fire-fighting:

Label the washing machineWe put a ‘WASH’ label on the right program, so guests don’t pick a 3-hour cycle. It saves energy, and many people don’t know how to use one.
Label how things workThe coffee machine, the heater… especially in shared apartments.
Photograph everythingElectricity box, boiler, heating controls, Wi-Fi router. Store the photos in your manual for when you need to explain something.
One extra set of protectorsSpare pillow protectors and mattress covers per property, so a bed is never left unprotected.
Stainless steel pansThey last longer and look clean for longer.
Stock up on small spoonsThey always go missing. Always.
Visual trash instructionsLabeled photos or icons that show guests exactly where and how to separate their waste.
Pro tip

“Something isn’t working”? Ask for a quick video first. Or jump on a video call before sending maintenance. Often it isn’t broken, it’s just being used the wrong way. This one step saves time, unnecessary callouts and helps you diagnose faster.

Section 5

The shared spaces special

Essential things you need to know

Shared apartments, where guests have private rooms but share the kitchen, bathroom or living room, can be very profitable. But they come with their own rules, systems and friction points. Here’s how to manage them smoothly:

Clear boundaries from day one

Add clear house rules to your listing.

Private vs. shared, in writing

Be specific in your listing and messages. Add photos, floor plans and the rules for shared areas (quiet hours, no personal items in common spaces).

A lock on every bedroom door

Lockable from inside and outside. Non-negotiable for safety, privacy and trust.

Dedicated, labeled spaces

Label shelves, drawers and even fridge sections in shared kitchens and bathrooms.

Clean more often

Even daily in high-turnover properties. Cleanliness is one of the top review killers in shared setups.

Keep extras

Towels, toilet paper, small utensils and mugs, so there’s enough for everyone.

Resolve conflicts fast

If one guest complains about another, respond fast, stay neutral and offer a solution, like changing rooms or reinforcing the rules. The quick replies in Lesson 9 have templates for this.

Pro tip: put a friendly house rules sign (or a mini welcome booklet) in the living room or kitchen. It’s a subtle way to guide behavior and avoid awkward situations.

The 3-step decluttering process for shared spaces

Over time, shared kitchens and bathrooms fill up with things previous guests left behind. That means mess, confusion and even hygiene issues. Reset and declutter at least every 3 months, without removing items that are still in use. First, pick your method:

Method A

The “lost & found” system

Choose one spot for leftover items, like a basket in the bathroom or a freezer drawer. Anything placed there is removed after a set deadline. Great for shampoo bottles, freezer food and forgotten belongings.

Method B

The label system

Leave tape and a marker near shared storage (fridge door, pantry). Guests label their items with their name. Anything unlabeled gets cleared out.

Key areas:Shower bottlesFreezer & fridge doorUnlabeled drawers & shelvesRandom items in common areas
1

Start with a deep clean

Clean the kitchen, bathroom and hallway. It’s the best moment to spot forgotten items, expired food and things taking up space. Then move them to your removal spot, or start labeling.

2

Communicate clearly and kindly

Even if you spoke to someone in person, send a message with the method and a short deadline. Send a reminder the day before you remove anything.

3

Set a clear removal date

Give people 48–72 hours to claim their things, then remove what’s left. Optional: let remaining items be “adopted” before they’re thrown away.

You can send these as a WhatsApp, Airbnb or group message after the deep clean:

Message template: declutter announcement
Edit the parts in [brackets], then copy. Your changes are saved on this device.
Message template: final reminder
Edit the parts in [brackets], then copy. Your changes are saved on this device.
Section 6

Routine property inspections

(every 6 months)

No matter how clean or well-managed your property is, wear and tear is inevitable. That’s why doing a full fix-up every 6 months is key to maintaining high standards, avoiding complaints, and keeping your property looking fresh and professional. This can be done by you or a manager.

This doesn’t have to be a massive renovation; think of it as a deep maintenance check-up.

Maintenance inspection
Cleaning inspection

Even with a great cleaner, some things can get overlooked over time. Do a surprise visit or ask your manager for a video call walk-through. Check these often-missed details:

This 6-month fix-up routine helps you:

✓ Prevent negative reviews✓ Keep your maintenance budget low✓ Maintain property value over time
Consistency is everything. Add a recurring reminder to your calendar and make it part of your hosting system. A well-maintained property keeps guests coming back.
Section 7

Bonus: checklists, property manual and inventory

Property inspection checklists

To maintain high standards across your properties, it's essential to have clear inspection systems in place. The Maintenance Checklist helps your manager spot and fix small issues before they turn into costly repairs, ensuring everything is functional, safe, and guest-ready.

Meanwhile, the Cleaning Inspection Checklist is designed to uphold your property's cleanliness, organization, and hygiene beyond the basic turnover by focusing on deeper tasks that are often overlooked. Both lists should be used regularly (at least once a month for maintenance and weekly for cleaning) to protect your property, impress guests, and reduce negative reviews.

Part 3 · Lesson 12

Automate for passive income

Self-check-in, what to automate, what to delegate.

4 sections · about 30 minLesson12
Section 1

How to set up self-check-in

(keys, locks, and codes)

Self-check-in is one of the best systems you can set up as a host. It saves time, reduces stress and lets guests arrive whenever it suits them, even in the middle of the night. Here’s how to make it smooth and secure, in 5 steps.

1

Choose your self-check-in method

Tap the method you will use:

Control everything remotely with a hubConnect your smart lock or smart doorbell to a Wi-Fi gateway or smart home hub (like the Nuki Bridge, the TTLock Gateway or Amazon Alexa). Then you can change codes and open the door from anywhere, without being there.
Key handoff tipWe use KeyNest for two of our apartments: guests collect the keys at partner shops, lockers or cafés nearby.
2

Where to place it

LockboxMounted securely to a wall, gate or railing near the entrance, well-lit at night, and shown in your check-in guide with photos.
Smart lockMake sure Wi-Fi or Bluetooth works well at the door, and test that the code works before the guest arrives.
3

Set up your codes

Smart lockA unique code per booking, active from check-in until checkout, plus a master code for emergencies.
LockboxChange the code from time to time, whenever needed (for example if you think it has been shared). Never use obvious codes like 0000 or 1234.
4

Create a foolproof check-in guide

Picture your guest: tired, maybe jet-lagged, standing outside a building they’ve never seen. Your instructions should be so clear that even a child could follow them.

  • Step-by-step instructions, from the front gate to the exact spot of the key box
  • Photos of the entrance, the lock and the path to the door, with arrows and markers
  • Wi-Fi, parking and anything they need before entering
  • The same steps written in your message too, even if you send images or a PDF
  • Sent the day before or the morning of check-in
AI shortcut: ask ChatGPT or Claude to turn your photos into a clear check-in guide with numbered steps, like this one.
5

Have a backup plan

Batteries die and codes stop working. Always have a plan B:

A hidden backup key nearbyA neighbor, co-host or manager close byA master code or manual override
Digital locksSuper convenient, but someone has to check and replace the batteries regularly. Great, as long as your team stays on top of it.
Physical keysThey get lost often. In Barcelona, guests sometimes lose them when their bags are stolen, and many forget to return them to the right spot.
Final note

Self-check-in is only stress-free when it works reliably. Test your system, update your instructions regularly, and always keep a backup key or contact ready.

Your tasks
Section 2

What to automate and what to delegate

The key to running your business with less stress is knowing what to automate, what to delegate and what truly needs you.

Automatethe repetitive
Delegatethe physical
Keepwhat grows the business

Automate: anything that happens the same way, again and again

Scheduled messages

Use scheduled messages in the Airbnb inbox for welcome messages, check-in info, checkout instructions, review requests and FAQ answers. Templates are in the bonus below.

Keep it simple. Could a 5-year-old understand it? Travelers have a short attention span. In the check-in message, share only what they need to get in. Local tips go in a separate link, or in a follow-up message the day after arrival.
Turn on “send for last-minute bookings and short stays”For essential messages, so last-minute guests still receive them, no matter when or how long they book.
Add your check-in photos to the messageAirbnb now allows photos in scheduled messages. Add your step-by-step check-in photos once, and every guest gets them automatically. Practically zero work for you.

Pricing

A dynamic pricing tool like PriceLabs, Wheelhouse or Beyond Pricing adjusts your nightly rates to demand, events and competition. Airbnb’s own rule sets can also raise or lower prices automatically, for example for last-minute discounts or high season.

Calendars, locks and cleaning

Calendar syncOn other platforms too (Booking.com, Vrbo)? Sync your calendars to avoid double bookings.
Smart locksCodes created remotely and activated or deactivated automatically per guest.
Cleaner calendar accessGive your cleaner the calendar view, so they always see upcoming bookings (without message access, so they can’t see your earnings).
Keep the conversation on Airbnb, not on WhatsApp

Don’t send guests to WhatsApp. You end up answering in two places, and only messages inside the Airbnb chat count for Airbnb’s support team. If there’s an incident, a conflict, or a guest claims you said something, messages outside Airbnb are not taken into account.

We only give a phone number for emergencies. When guests still write there for the check-in instructions, we answer with one line and then reply properly in the Airbnb chat:

You, on WhatsAppThis is an emergency number. I’ll reply to you in the Airbnb chat.

That sets the boundary. From then on, the guest talks to you on Airbnb.

Delegate: anything that requires physical presence or personal interaction

You shouldn’t be cleaning your own property or doing late-night check-ins. Build a team you trust for everything on-site:

Cleaning & laundryA reliable cleaner and a standard checklist, so it’s done the same way every time.
MaintenanceSomeone on call for small repairs, broken appliances and emergencies.
Guest supportWant to step away fully? A co-host or manager answers messages, coordinates cleaning and solves issues.
RestockingWeekly or monthly, with a working capital and receipt tracking.
Keep for yourself, at least at first

The foundation you set yourself

Doing these yourself at the start teaches you the business inside out, so you can delegate them clearly later:

Guest experience & tone of voiceBranding & listing optimizationReviews & reputationSystems: SOPs, templates, trackers
The recipe for scaling with freedom

Automate the repetitive. Delegate the physical. Spend your time on what actually grows the business: branding, strategy and experience.

Your tasks
Section 3

Communication systems for your team

Clear communication is the backbone of a smooth operation, especially with several people involved: cleaners, a handyman, a manager. Without systems, things fall through the cracks.

One group per property

A WhatsApp group (or your preferred app) with everyone involved, named like [Property name] – Operations team. Use it for:

  • Schedule coordination
  • Guest updates (late checkouts, early check-ins)
  • Damage or missing items, with photos
  • Receipts and the remaining working capital

Access to the property wiki

Your team should always have the wiki (see bonus template), with:

Cleaning checklistSupply listProduct linksEmergency contactsAppliance how-tosWalkthrough videos

No more repeating yourself, and faster onboarding.

Response times

Agree when and how fast people reply. For example:

  • Cleaners confirm checkouts within 2 hours
  • The emergency contact is reachable by phone while guests are on-site
  • The manager sends a daily update when needed

Pinned messages & folders

Pin the key info (door codes, checklists, payment info) to the top of the group. For bigger systems, use a shared Google Drive or Dropbox folder.

Voice notes when helpful

Not everything needs to be typed. For longer updates or walk-throughs, a quick voice note saves time and feels more human.

Clarity = fewer mistakes. Miscommunication causes missed cleanings and bad guest experiences. The clearer your systems, the smoother your operations, and the less you’re needed day to day.
Your tasks
Section 4

Bonus: scheduled messages that feel personal

Scheduled messages save you time but that doesn’t mean they should feel robotic. The key is to write them in a warm, friendly tone and include personal touches like the guest’s name.

When done right, scheduled messages feel like genuine communication while ensuring every guest gets the info they need on time, every time.

How to set them up
  • Where they go: in Airbnb, under “Scheduled messages”. Each one has a trigger and a time, shown above its title here.
  • Automatic: once saved, Airbnb sends them to every guest on its own. Use Airbnb’s shortcodes for the guest’s first name so each message feels personal.
  • Add your check-in photos to message 2, so the guest gets the pictures without you sending anything.

Part 3 · Lesson 13

Scale up to 6 figures

When to expand, multiple countries, staying legal.

5 sections · about 15 minLesson13
Section 1

When to expand (and when to wait)

Deciding to expand is one of the most exciting milestones in your hosting journey. But growing too fast or too soon can backfire. Be honest with yourself and tick what’s true today:

Are you ready to expand?
✓ You’re ready to expand if:
✕ You should wait if:

Optimize before you expand. Expanding too soon is one of the most common mistakes new hosts make. A second listing should feel like a natural next step, not a leap of faith.
Your tasks
Section 2

Managing multiple listings from different countries

Hosting in several countries lets you diversify your income, tap into different markets and earn year-round. We do it with Barcelona and Bali. It works, as long as you plan for time zones, local rules and remote teams.

Build strong local teams

You can’t be everywhere, so your on-the-ground team is everything:

Cleaner + backupLocal handymanManager or co-hostNearby emergency contact

Find, test and train them well. Once they’re solid, your properties run with minimal input.

Standardize everything

The same systems in every property, so the next one is a copy, not a new project:

  • Cleaning checklists
  • Guest message templates
  • Restock trackers
  • SOPs for turnovers and emergencies

The bonus templates are made for this.

Automate across time zones

  • Scheduled messages keep communication consistent
  • Dynamic pricing (PriceLabs, Beyond) adapts to each local market
  • Smart locks remove the need to be there
  • Check that messages go out in the guest’s time zone, not at 3am

Know the local laws and taxes

Every country has its own licenses, registrations and taxes (VAT, tourist tax). Hire a local accountant or legal advisor where needed. More on this in the next section.

Separate your finances

A separate bank account, payment method and working capital per property. You’ll see how each one performs, and taxes in each country get simpler.

Protect your time and sanity

Batch tasks by time zone, keep one WhatsApp group per property (Lesson 12), and consider a virtual assistant to watch messages while you sleep.

Our advice

Start with one country and build solid systems. Once your first international listing runs without your constant involvement, you have a blueprint to copy anywhere. Treat it like a business, not a hobby.

Your tasks
Section 3

Staying legally compliant while scaling

One listing is simple. Several cities or countries? Compliance gets more complex, and more important. You already know the basics from Lesson 2. Here’s your checklist for every new location:

1

Research the local rental laws

Are short stays legal here?Night limits per year?Zoning restrictions?Do you need to live on-site?
Ask localsLocal host Facebook groups and the Airbnb Community Center are great for hearing about recent changes.
2

Get the right licenses and registrations

Many cities require a business license, a short-term rental permit, a registration number on your listing and emergency contact info on-site. Without them: hefty fines or removal from the platform. Check the municipality’s website or ask a local attorney.

3

Understand your taxes

You may oweTourist or occupancy tax, income tax (local and foreign if you manage from abroad), and VAT or sales tax in some countries.
You may need toRegister as a business, file monthly or quarterly returns, and keep every receipt and expense report.

Work with an accountant who knows short-term rentals in each country you operate in.

4

Follow guest safety rules

Smoke & CO detectorsFire extinguisherFirst-aid kitMarked exitsInsurance

Even where it’s not mandatory, it protects you and your guests, and may be needed for Airbnb’s host protection.

5

Track legal changes

Short-term rental laws change constantly. What’s legal today might not be tomorrow. Set up Google Alerts, follow local news and stay connected with other hosts.

Bonus tip: keep digital copies of every permit, license and tax receipt in one shared folder (Google Drive or Notion), so you can find them anytime.
Your tasks
Section 4

Bonus: property finance tracker

Whether you have one property or ten, tracking your finances is essential. It shows you exactly how much you’re earning and spending, which costs you can cut, and which property (or month) earns the most. It also makes your tax return a lot easier. Update it once a month and you’ll always know where your business stands.

Property finance tracker

Income, expenses and profit per property. Always update it monthly.

Make your own copy

Profit & ROI calculator

Smart hosts run the numbers first, emotion comes second.

Tool$

Before signing a lease or investing in furniture, it’s crucial to understand your numbers. This Profit & ROI Calculator helps you estimate how much income a property can generate and how long it will take to earn back your initial investment.

It’s designed to give you a quick, realistic snapshot of: monthly and yearly profit, return on investment (ROI), break-even timeline, and how your numbers shift at different occupancy rates.

How to use it
  1. Step 1: choose your currency and fill in your business expenses.
  2. Step 2: pick your business model and enter your numbers under “Enter your data here”. The tables update automatically.
  3. Review the results at different occupancy rates (70%, 85%, 95%) to see how scenarios play out.

For more explanation of a field, tap “What is this?” under it. Your numbers are saved on this device.

Calculate your business expenses first. If you need help estimating any costs, use the AI prompt below. Once completed, your expenses automatically flow into the three calculators in step 2.

AI prompt: estimate my costs
You are a short-term rental business expert. I am planning a short-term rental property in , with [# BEDROOMS] bedrooms, cleaned [CLEANING FREQUENCY PER MONTH] times per month. Please give me realistic average monthly and one-time cost estimates for this destination, based on typical short-term rental operations. Use for all numbers. Break down the costs in the following structure: Monthly expenses: Utilities (electricity, gas if applicable, internet, water, insurance), Team (cleaner based on the cleaning frequency above, handyman, property manager if commonly used in this destination, pool cleaner if applicable, gardener if applicable, accountant / admin), Other monthly expenses (supplies such as toiletries and consumables based on turnover, maintenance reserve). One-time setup costs: Kitchen setup, living room setup, bedroom setup, bathroom setup, laundry setup, outdoor / pool area if applicable. For each cost, provide: - A realistic average range (low–high) - A recommended estimate to use for financial planning Also mention: - Any costs that are commonly underestimated in this destination - Whether costs are higher or lower than average compared to similar markets Keep the answer practical, realistic, and suitable for plugging directly into a profit & ROI calculator.

What is this?
This is the price that guests will pay for your room per night. To estimate the nightly rate, we recommend doing two types of research:
  • Check similar listings on the Airbnb platform.
  • Use a market data tool like AirROI to review local metrics.
Airbnb applies platform fees and taxes of approximately 17%, depending on the country. These fees are typically paid by the guest. Therefore, the prices you see on Airbnb as a traveler usually already include this additional 17%.

Occupancy rateMonthly incomeMonthly costsMonthly profitYearly profitROIBreak even
%Worst-case

What do the columns mean?

Occupancy rate. The occupancy rate is the percentage of nights your place is booked. For example: if your property gets booked for 15 days in the month and the other 15 days are not rented, your occupancy rate is 50%. Worst-case, average and best-case are the worst, average and best occupancy in the zone where you are going to start. You can change each percentage.

Monthly income. How much you would earn per month before deducting any expenses — also called gross income.

Monthly costs. The costs to manage a property: cleaners, cleaning products, handyman services, utility bills (water, electricity, gas, internet) ... You can change them in step 1.

Monthly profit. Your estimated income after subtracting all recurring monthly costs, such as rent, team, utilities and cleaning costs.

ROI. Your yearly return on investment, as a percentage.

Break even. How long (in months) it will take to recover your initial investment.

Occupancy rate. The occupancy rate is the percentage of nights your place is booked. *A leasehold is when you rent a property long-term, often for several years, with the right to use it as your own. In places like Bali, foreigners can’t own land, so leaseholds are the most common way to legally control and profit from a property without actually buying it. You pay upfront or yearly, and in return, you get full use of the property for the length of the lease.

Bonus · for guests & team

Label system

What to label, how to do it, and a printable label sheet.

Tools★

Labels are one of the cheapest ways to save time. They keep your team organized and answer guests’ questions before they ask. More about this in Lesson 11.

Clear labeling helps your team stay organized, reduces guest confusion, and saves time during turnovers.

Why labels matter:

  • Ensure all items go back in the right place
  • Help new team members quickly understand the system
  • Make your space more intuitive for guests
  • Avoid loss or misuse of supplies
  • Reduce daily questions and communication

What to Label:

For guests:

  • Fridge shelves (label with room/suite names or numbers)
  • Kitchen cabinets or drawers (clearly mark shared vs. private)
  • Water dispensers (e.g. “Drinking Water Only”)
  • Trash & recycling bins
  • Which program you recommend on the washing machine
  • Bathroom storage areas (“Shared” / “Private”)

For staff use:

  • Cleaning product shelves or boxes
  • Supply restock bins (e.g. “spare towels”, “toilet paper stock”)
  • Lost & Found box
  • Garden tools or pool supply storage
  • Instructions for wash cycles on the washing machine
  • Laundry room baskets (e.g. “dirty towels”, “stained sheets”, “ready to wash”)

Label Tips:

  • Use laminated or waterproof labels in kitchens, bathrooms, and outdoor areas.
  • For visual clarity, include icons or color codes if your team includes non-native speakers. Here is a website with free icons that you can use: www.flaticon.com
  • Make sure all labels are consistent in font, size, and wording.
  • Labels sometimes need to be renewed. Therefore, it's useful to invest in a laminating machine or label maker. It doesn't need to be an expensive one, just a simple one will do.
  • KEEP IT SIMPLE! Stick to clear, simple wording: e.g., “Suite 1 Shelf”, “Refills Only”, “Not for Guests”. Don’t add multiple languages, because too much text gets overwhelming. Use one language (for example English) plus icons or images.

Little details that save big headaches

  • Label the washing machine programs so your team knows exactly which setting to use. A ‘WASH’ label on the right program stops guests from picking a 3-hour cycle.
  • Label how things work, like the coffee machine or the heater, especially in shared apartments.
  • Label shelves, drawers and fridge sections in shared kitchens and bathrooms, so every guest knows their space.
🏷️ Make your own labels

Write one label per line. Then download the sheet, print it on paper or sticker paper, and laminate the labels for kitchens, bathrooms and outdoor areas.

Bonus · for shared properties

Declutter shared spaces

A simple 3-step process, with ready-to-send messages.

Tools★

In shared spaces, guests leave things behind: food in the fridge, bottles in the shower, random items in the hallway. This 3-step process keeps everything clean and fair. More about shared spaces in Lesson 11.

Tip: it’s good to do this at least every 3 months.

Over time, shared spaces like the kitchen and bathroom can get cluttered with items left behind by previous guests or tenants, especially in longer stays or co-living setups. This creates mess, confusion, and even hygiene issues.

To maintain a clean, welcoming space for everyone, it’s important to periodically reset and declutter. Here’s a simple system you can use to clear shared areas without causing misunderstandings or tension.

There are two main approaches that we recommend to avoid removing items that are still in use.

The “lost & found” system

Designate a specific spot for unclaimed or leftover items, like a basket in the bathroom or a drawer in the freezer. Let guests know that anything placed there will be removed after a set deadline.

This method works especially well for things like shampoo bottles, freezer items, or personal belongings left in shared spaces.

The label system

Place a roll of tape and a marker near shared storage areas (like the fridge door or pantry). Ask guests to label their items with their name. Anything left unlabeled will be cleared out.

Key areas to declutter:

  • Shampoo and soap bottles in the shower
  • Freezer and fridge door
  • Unlabeled drawers and shelves
  • Random items in common areas

Start with a deep clean

Start with a full cleaning of shared areas, especially the kitchen, bathroom, and hallway. This is the best time to spot forgotten items, expired food, or things taking up unnecessary space. Depending on the decluttering method you choose, either place these items in a designated removal spot or start labeling them with tape and a marker.

Communicate clearly & kindly

Even if you've spoken to someone in person, follow up with a message to set clear expectations and avoid any surprises. Include a short deadline and explain the decluttering method to identify or collect their items. Make sure to send a reminder the day before you are removing the items.

Set a clear removal date

Give a 48–72 hour window for people to claim their belongings. After that, remove everything left behind. Optional: allow remaining items to be “adopted” before discarding eg: this is the last chance to collect your items. Anything still here after [time] is free to be taken or will be discarded.

You can send this as a WhatsApp, Airbnb or group message after a deep clean:

© 2026 6 Figure Host. All rights reserved. For individual use only.Privacy policy
Bonus · protect your peace

Difficult guests

Kind, but firm. How to reply when a guest keeps pushing for more.

Bonus★

Most guests are lovely. But a small group will test you: they ask for discounts, push for exceptions or argue about the rules. How you reply decides how far it goes.

Why being too nice backfires

You want to help, so you bend a little. A small discount, an early check-in, one exception. With most guests that’s fine. But some read it as weakness, not kindness. One favor becomes the next request, and then the next one.

In the end you gave more, you got more stress, and you still feel disappointed. Often the review is not even better.

What they hear

“Let me see what I can do…”
“OK, just this once.”
“I’m so sorry, of course…”
= there is room to negotiate.

What works

“Our price for these dates is as listed.”
“This is our policy for every guest.”
“Here is what we can do.”
= clear, calm, final.

Reply like a company, not a friend

With difficult guests, sound a bit like a robot. Friendly, but neutral. You are a business with rules, not a person who can be talked into favors.

1

Keep it short

One to three sentences. No long stories, no emotions, no jokes when things are tense.

2

Point to the rules

Your house rules, cancellation policy and listing description do the talking. “These are the rules for every guest.”

3

Don’t over-explain

Every extra sentence is something new to argue with. The more you write, the more you feed it.

4

Fix the problem, not the price

Is something really wrong? Offer a fix once: fresh towels, a repair, a cleaner. Not a discount.

5

Stay on the platform

Keep every message in Airbnb. If it ends up with support, they can see the whole conversation.

The three-message rule

When a guest keeps arguing, don’t get pulled into a long chat. Use this ladder and stop at step three.

1

Answer once, clearly

State the rule and what you can offer. Friendly and short.

2

Repeat it, shorter

Same answer, fewer words. Nothing new to argue with.

3

End the conversation

Close it politely and point to Airbnb support. Then stop replying.

The line that always works

“I’m going to end this conversation now. This is our policy, and it is the same for every guest. From now on, you can contact Airbnb support directly, and they will help you further.”

Keep your word

When you say you’ll end the conversation, end it. If you keep replying after that, you lose your authority and the situation grows. Only reply again for a safety issue or a real new problem during the stay.

When it really gets out of hand

Rude messages, insults, threats? You don’t have to take it. Say it calmly, end it, and let Airbnb support take over. They can talk to the guest for you and help find a solution.

The line that always works

“I don’t feel comfortable continuing this conversation, so I’m going to end it here. You can contact Airbnb support, and they will help us find a solution.”

Remember: you are never alone. Airbnb support can step in, message the guest and decide on refunds, so you don’t have to carry the fight yourself.

Example conversations

Three situations every host meets sooner or later, and short replies that keep you in control.

Example

The discount request

Guest

Hi! Love your place. Can you offer a discount for 5 nights?

You

Hi Marco, thanks for your message! Our price for these dates is as listed, and it includes a lot: one of the most central locations in the city, weekly cleaning, towels and bed sheets. Hope to welcome you!

Guest

Come on, it’s low season. Give us a discount?

You

You’re welcome to stay! 😊 Unfortunately, we don’t offer additional discounts, as this is already our best rate for long-term stays.

The room is worth its price thanks to its location in one of the best and most central areas of Barcelona, and the amenities: weekly cleaning of the shared spaces, towels, bed sheets and everything you need to feel at home are already included.

What also sets us apart from other Airbnbs is our focus on great service, fast communication and a clean, well-managed home.

We’d love to host you, and if you have any other questions, ask away!

Why it works No discount, no “maybe”, but a reason to book: you remind them what the price includes. A guest who keeps pushing for a discount often brings more problems. It’s fine to let them go.

You’ll find this reply in our message templates (Lesson 9) →

Example

A small flaw becomes a discount demand

Guest

One towel had a stain. I think we deserve a discount.

You

Thanks for letting us know, sorry about that! Our team will bring fresh towels within the hour.

Guest

That’s not enough. Our review will reflect our experience if you don’t give us a discount.

You

The towels have been replaced. We don’t give discounts for this. Airbnb doesn’t allow reviews to be used to ask for a discount or refund. If you disagree, you can contact Airbnb support.

Why it works Fix the real problem fast, then hold the line. Using a review to get a discount breaks Airbnb’s rules, so take a screenshot and report it.

Example

The early check-in request

Guest

Can we have an early check-in? Our flight arrives at 08:00.

You

Welcome! Check-in is from 3pm, because the room needs to be cleaned and prepared for every new guest. You’re welcome to drop off your luggage from 11am. Arriving earlier? There is a luggage storage point a 5-minute walk from the apartment, so you can explore the city without your bags.

Guest

But we’ll be exhausted after the flight. Can’t you make an exception?

You

I understand. Check-in stays at 3pm, the same for every guest. Your luggage is welcome with us from 11am.

Why it works Say no to what you can’t give, and yes to what you can: a place for their bags. The second time, the same answer, shorter.

Our luggage storage replies are in the message templates (Lesson 9) →

Real case: two guests, one living room

From one of our colivings in Barcelona

One guest (room 6) told us the couch right outside her room was used all day for work calls, and in the evenings for movies and music. Nobody broke the quiet hours after 10pm, but through the thin wall she heard everything, almost every day.

  1. We sent a friendly message to all housemates, without names: take calls in your room and use the other couch.
    See the message
    You · to all housemates

    Hi everyone! 😊

    We hope you’re well. We wanted to let you know that noise from the couch near Room 6 can easily be heard inside the bedroom, even during the day, and if it’s daily it can be a lot. Even if quiet times after 10pm are respected.

    Therefore we’d kindly ask you, in case you have (work) calls, to take them in the bedroom if possible, and rather use the couch on the other side of the living room when hanging out or listening to music. Feel free to move the lounge chairs there too, so that we can give Room 6 a break from the noise. Especially during weekdays.

    Of course, everyone is welcome to enjoy the common areas! We just want to make sure everyone feels comfortable.

    Thank you so much!

  2. The guest taking the calls (room 4) hit back with a long list about the other guest: the kitchen, the bathroom, shoes inside, being unpleasant.
    See the message
    Bréanne, room 4

    Hi,

    I would like to report the appalling and inconsiderate behavior of the person in Room 6. In addition to being somewhat unclean (she messes up the bathroom and leaves the kitchen somewhat unclean, for example by not cleaning her pan all day yesterday), she is extremely unpleasant and, for example, tells me and the other flatmates to be quiet on a Sunday at 9pm when we are having dinner together.

    Clearly, this person doesn’t want a roommate, yet she chose a shared apartment. She will therefore have to get used to it. The common areas are accessible to everyone, and the other roommates and I have always respected the quiet hours (from 10pm). In this case, it’s she who will have to deal with the fact that there are other people in the house. I booked this Airbnb to share my experience in Barcelona with other people. Apart from her, everything is going great. If she wants to stay in a hotel by herself, she should do so.

    She is very unpleasant and speaks to us rudely. The last time the housekeeper knocked on her door, she spoke rudely to her too. She needs to calm down and learn to be respectful. 😅

    She also puts her belongings in places that don’t belong to her (for example, her bottle of red wine in the compartment to the right of Room 1). I didn’t mention it to you to try not to create any tension, but now it’s starting to be a lot, especially if she’s complaining on top of that…

  3. It escalated: a call outside the room close to 11pm, a slammed door, and “buy earplugs”.
    See the message
    Guest, room 6

    Can you please pass on the messages? I now have a girl taking a call outside my room, and it is almost 11pm!

    It is the girl in room 4 who is always on the couch. I’ve now asked her to move twice. She hasn’t listened, just told me to get earplugs… This is really unacceptable now. Please can you sort this, or I’ll need to find another solution. It’s very uncomfortable for me.

  4. Then we took a clear position: one simple solution (calls on the other couch or at the big desk), what was not OK (“telling her to use earplugs is rude”), and the consequence (if it continues, we contact Airbnb, and they may cancel reservations for conflict between guests).
    See the message

    This is the most important message. We said we weren’t judging and that we had heard both sides, but we were clear about the rules and what she had to do. Firm, strict, with authority.

    You · the key message

    Hi Bréanne,

    Apparently you are still taking loud calls on the couch next to the room, and she said the situation got even worse.

    It’s clear that there is a lot of built-up frustration on both sides, and we are not there, so we’re not judging.

    But this tension has to stop.

    There is a very easy solution: simply use the other couch for calls (or any other place in the apartment), even during the day. So we kindly ask you to make this effort.

    Telling her to use earplugs is rude and not a solution.

    If not, we will have to contact Airbnb, and they might end up cancelling both reservations for conflict between guests, which is something we want to avoid.

    We hope we can count on you, and that we don’t receive any more complaints from either side.

  5. She replied with a long message, explaining everything again.
    See the message
    Bréanne, room 4

    I’m at the living room table, not on the sofa. I’m willing to make an effort, but the living room isn’t hers either, and she acts like it is.

    I’m willing to make an effort by going to the table that’s further away, but at some point I need to be able to work in the apartment without it being a problem.

    I mentioned earplugs to her because it seems she can’t even stand a normal conversation in the living room. That’s not normal. We don’t shout with the other flatmates either, and apart from her, no one has complained. The guest who had her room before also used to work from home with me, and it never caused the slightest problem.

    She explains everything again. We don’t. One more firm message, and the conversation is over.

  6. We didn’t explain ourselves again: one more firm message, and we ended the conversation. She moved to the desk, the other guest thanked us, and there were no more complaints.
    See the conversation
    You

    Even though we accept working in the apartment, you have to keep in mind that its first goal is a place to live, not a coworking.

    The apartment is big enough to both work and not create noise for room 6.

    You can also use the big desk instead of the table, which is set up for working and even further away.

    I am going to end this conversation now. No need to reply. We have heard and understand both sides. All we want is no more complaints.

    Bréanne, room 4

    Okay, I’ll use the far desk to show my good faith. Have a good day, and again, I’m sorry for all this.

    You

    Thank you so much! Have a great day.

    The next day

    Bréanne, room 4

    Thank you so much for the lamps! The gentleman came by :)

    You

    So glad it’s fixed 🙌🏻

What we learned

  • Listen to both sides. You weren’t there, so don’t judge.
  • Start with one message for everyone, without names.
  • Never send the problem back to the guests. You are the host: decide.
  • Give one concrete solution and one clear consequence.
  • End the conversation, then stay kind. The next day we fixed her lamps, and she thanked us.

Airbnb’s rules are on your side

Review threats

Guests may not threaten a negative review to get a refund, money or other benefits. Don’t give in. Keep it in Airbnb messages, take a screenshot and contact support. If the review is posted anyway, you can ask Airbnb to remove it.

Airbnb’s reviews policy

“Pay me outside Airbnb”

Guests and hosts may not offer or ask for discounts to book outside Airbnb. Decline it: you lose all protection, and it can cost you your listing.

Airbnb’s off-platform policy

Reviews after a difficult stay

Reviews are hidden until both of you have written one, or until the 14-day review window closes. So after a tense stay, protect yourself.

1

Be honest, not nice

Did the guest break rules, insult you or your team, or try to pressure you? Rate what really happened, low stars included. Don’t feel bad: it protects you and warns the next host.

2

Changed your mind? Remove it

If the guest ends up leaving you a great review and your rating feels too harsh, you can remove your own review within 30 days of publishing: Profile → Reviews → reviews you’ve written → Remove review.

3

Never trade reviews

Don’t offer or accept deals like “I remove mine if you remove yours”. Airbnb doesn’t allow hosts and guests to coordinate or pressure each other about reviews. Is the guest’s review unfair, retaliatory or a threat for money? Ask Airbnb to remove it.

How to remove a review

Spot it before they book

  • Their first message is a discount request.
  • They want to pay or talk outside the platform.
  • They ask for exceptions to your rules before they even booked.
  • They are vague about the number of guests or the reason for the trip.
One red flag is not a reason to decline. Two or three together? Trust your gut. Using “Request to book” lets you read the first message before you accept.

Protect your peace

It’s not personal

A guest testing your limits says more about them than about you or your place.

Decide your rules in advance

Write your replies before you need them. Then you answer from your rules, not from your mood.

Some people can’t be helped

You can’t make everyone happy. Be fair, be consistent, and let the platform handle the rest.

AI prompt: turn my reply into a calm, firm message
Act as a professional guest-relations manager for a short-term rental. A guest sent me this message: [paste the guest’s message] This is my rule or policy: [e.g. checkout is at 11:00 / no discounts on listed prices] What I can offer (optional): [e.g. luggage storage until 3pm] Write a reply of maximum three short sentences. Friendly but neutral, like a company. Don’t apologize too much, don’t over-explain, don’t offer a discount, and don’t open new topics. Also give me a shorter second version in case they keep arguing, and a final message that politely ends the conversation and refers them to Airbnb support.
Copy and open in:ChatGPTGeminiClaude
The takeaway

Kind to everyone, firm with the few. Short replies, clear rules, and when you say the conversation is over, it’s over.
